Network Realignment Complexes over General Graphs

Fabienne Klatt , Iason Papadopoulos and Marc Raffelsiefen F. Klatt, I. Papadopoulos, and M. Raffelsiefen
Department of Mathematics
University of Bremen
Bibliothekstraße 5
28359 Bremen
Germany Email address, F. Klatt : faklatt@uni-bremen.de Email address, I. Papadopoulos : iason@uni-bremen.de Email address, M. Raffelsiefen : mraffels@uni-bremen.de
Abstract.

Network realignment complexes were introduced by Kozlov [16]. We generalise their definition to arbitrary connected base graphs.

For a connected graph GG, we characterise the connected components of the associated network realignment complex XGX_{G} and show that XGX_{G} admits an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction onto the disjoint union of a complete graph and a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space. For the complete base graph KnK_{n}, we study the metric structure of the network realignment graph 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} and obtain explicit upper and lower bounds for its diameter. Finally, we prove that XnX_{n} is a cubical flag complex and that every automorphism of XnX_{n} is induced by a relabelling of the underlying vertex set. In particular, Aut⁡(Xn)≅Sn\Aut(X_{n})\cong S_{n} for all n≥5n\geq 5.

Introduction

Reconfiguration problems study how one configuration can be transformed into another through a sequence of small changes while maintaining validity at every step. This is modelled by a reconfiguration graph, whose vertices represent configurations and whose edges correspond to elementary transitions, called reconfiguration steps, between them [11].

A fundamental question in reconfiguration concerns connectivity [20]. Can any configuration be transformed into any other by a sequence of elementary transitions? If not, which configurations can be reached from a given starting configuration? Equivalently, how can the connected components of the reconfiguration graph be characterised?

This naturally leads to a second fundamental question: given two configurations in the same connected component, what is the length of a shortest sequence of elementary transitions between them? Further, can the distance between any two connected realignments be bounded? In the case where the reconfiguration graph is connected, this corresponds to determining its diameter [21].

In this paper, the configurations are spanning trees of a fixed base graph. The reconfiguration step is given by the leaf slide, that is a leaf is detached from its parent and reconnected to a vertex adjacent to that parent. Two spanning trees are adjacent in the reconfiguration graph if they differ by a leaf slide. The resulting reconfiguration graph is called network realignment graph.

A natural extension of the reconfiguration framework is to allow multiple reconfiguration steps to be performed simultaneously, provided that they are independent of each other (or, more suggestively, the corresponding operations commute) [9]. This idea results in a cubical complex whose 1-skeleton is the reconfiguration graph. In the setting of network realignments, this introduces higher-dimensional cubes to the network realignment graph, leading to the network realignment complex.

This viewpoint naturally shifts the focus from connectivity of the reconfiguration graph to higher connectivity, i.e. the topology of the associated network realignment complex. In particular, one may ask whether any two sequences of leaf slides connecting the same pair of spanning trees can themselves be transformed into one another.

Related Work. Ito et al. [11] gave a systematic complexity-theoretic treatment of reconfiguration problems. Nishimura [20] surveys both the structural and algorithmic aspects of reconfiguration, including reachability, connectivity, shortest-transformation problems, and the diameter of reconfiguration graphs. These works provide the general framework in which the network realignment graph may be viewed, although their results do not directly address the particular transformation of spanning trees considered here.

More closely related are reconfiguration graphs whose states are the spanning trees of a fixed connected graph GG. The tree graph 𝒯⁡(G)\mathcal{T}(G) has one vertex for each spanning tree of GG, with two spanning trees adjacent whenever one is obtained from the other by deleting one edge and inserting another. Cummins [4] studied Hamiltonian cycles in tree graphs. Their vertex-connectivity was subsequently investigated by Liu [18], while Estivill-Castro, Noy, and Urrutia [6] studied the chromatic numbers of tree graphs and of a restricted variant.

Several restrictions of the ordinary edge-exchange move have also been considered. In the adjacency tree graph, the deleted and inserted edges are additionally required to be adjacent in GG. Liu [17] studied the vertex-connectivity of adjacency tree graphs. An even more restrictive transformation gives the leaf-exchange spanning tree graph: the deleted and inserted edges must be incident with the same vertex, which is required to be a leaf in both spanning trees. Broersma and Li [3] characterised the connected graphs whose leaf-exchange spanning tree graph is connected and studied its connectivity. Kaneko and Yoshimoto [15] continued this investigation for 22-connected base graphs.

Every leaf slide considered in the present paper is a leaf-exchange, but the converse need not hold. In addition to preserving the same leaf, a leaf slide requires the old and new parents of that leaf to be joined by an edge of the current spanning tree. Thus, for a fixed connected base graph GG, these graphs form the following chain of inclusions.

tree graph⊇adjacency tree graph⊇leaf-exchange graph⊇network realignment graph\text{tree graph}\supseteq\text{adjacency tree graph}\supseteq\text{leaf-exchange graph}\supseteq\text{network realignment graph}

The tree graph, adjacency tree graph, leaf-exchange graph, and related constructions are reviewed by Ozeki and Yamashita [22].

A related line of research considers graphs with a fixed number of vertices and edges, where a local move replaces one edge by another through an edge move, edge rotation, or edge slide. Goddard and Swart [10] and Jarrett [12] study the metrics on the resulting reconfiguration graphs.

Another approach considers topological spaces constructed from graphs. Lovász [19] introduced the neighbourhood complex of a graph and used its connectivity to obtain lower bounds for the chromatic number. Babson and Kozlov [2] studied the more general complexes Hom⁡(H,G)\operatorname{Hom}(H,G), whose cells are graph multihomomorphisms from HH to GG. Jonsson [13] surveys simplicial complexes arising from graph families closed under edge deletion.

The construction most closely related to network realignment complexes is the state complex of a reconfigurable system. Ghrist and Peterson [9] associate a cubical complex to a system governed by local moves, where vertices represent states, edges represent individual moves, and higher-dimensional cubes encode collections of independent local moves. They study structural properties of these state complexes and spaces of reconfiguration paths using tools from CAT(0)(0) geometry. For a later treatment of state complexes as a class of cube complexes, see Peterson [23].

The direct predecessor of the present work is Kozlov’s network realignment complex [16], which corresponds to the case of the complete base graph KnK_{n}. Using discrete Morse theory, Kozlov proves that the resulting complex XnX_{n} is homotopy equivalent to the complete graph KnK_{n}.

Our Contribution. The main objective of this work is to investigate the topology and geometry of the network realignment graph and the associated cubical complex, with particular emphasis on the symmetries induced by automorphisms of the underlying base graph. Our results address these aspects from several complementary perspectives.

We begin with the topology of the network realignment complex XGX_{G} associated with an arbitrary connected base graph GG. In contrast to the complete graph case, the resulting reconfiguration graph need not be connected. We completely characterise the connected components of XGX_{G}, and show that it admits an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction onto the disjoint union of a complete graph and a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space, where the vertices of the complete graph are indexed by those spanning trees of GG that are star trees.

Next, we investigate the geometry of the network realignment graph. We restrict to the complete graph KnK_{n} and study the metric structure of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. In particular, we establish general upper and lower bounds for its diameter, partially answering an open problem posed in [16]. Our analysis also reveals several structural properties of the metric, including the role of star trees as central configurations and a characterisation of extremal trees. We also show that 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is bipartite if and only if nn is even.

Finally, we determine the automorphism group of the network realignment complex XnX_{n}. As an intermediate result, we prove that XnX_{n} is a cubical flag complex, i.e. is completely determined by its 1-skeleton, the network realignment graph 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. This allows us to show that every automorphism of XnX_{n} is induced by a permutation of the underlying vertex set, and hence

Aut⁡(Xn)≅Sn\Aut(X_{n})\cong S_{n}

for all n≥5n\geq 5.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 1, we introduce the network realignment graph and the associated cubical complex. Section 2 is devoted to the topology of the network realignment complex over an arbitrary base graph. After introducing the necessary tools from equivariant generalised Morse theory, we characterise the connected components of XGX_{G} and determine their Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant homotopy types. We conclude the section with several illustrative examples. Section 3 investigates the geometry of the network realignment graph associated with the complete graph, establishing bounds on its diameter together with further structural properties of the induced metric. Finally, in Section 4, we determine the automorphism group of the network realignment complex XnX_{n}.

Methodology. The proofs combine techniques from graph theory, discrete Morse theory, and combinatorial optimisation. The topological results rely on the equivariant generalised discrete Morse theory of Freij [8], building on Forman’s discrete Morse theory [7]. A key technical ingredient is an extension of Freij’s equivariant generalised discrete Morse theory to the present setting, developed in Section 2.1, allowing us to construct Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retractions of the network realignment complex.

Acknowledgement. We are grateful to Professor Feichtner-Kozlov for proposing this research topic and for many insightful comments and valuable suggestions provided throughout this project.

1. Network Realignment Complexes over General Base Graphs

In this section, we introduce the network realignment complex over general base graphs. Before presenting the definition, we fix some basic graph-theoretic notation.

Let GG be a finite simple undirected connected graph on n≥3n\geq 3 vertices. Then V⁡(G)V(G) denotes the set of vertices and E(G)⊆{(v,w)∣v,w∈V(G)}E(G)\subseteq\{(v,w)\mid v,w\in V(G)\} the set of edges. In the following, we will refer to GG as the base graph. Let G∖{v}G\setminus\{v\} denote the graph obtained from GG by deleting the vertex vv and all incident edges, and let G∖{e}G\setminus\{e\} denote the graph obtained from GG by deleting the edge ee. Given two subgraphs H1,H2H_{1},H_{2}, write H1∪H2=(V⁡(H1)∪V⁡(H2),E⁡(H1)∪E⁡(H2))H_{1}\cup H_{2}=(V(H_{1})\cup V(H_{2}),E(H_{1})\cup E(H_{2})). Let KnK_{n} denote the complete graph on nn vertices, and let sis_{i} denote the star tree with unique interior vertex ii and all other vertices adjacent to ii. For a vertex vv, let 𝒩G​(v)\mathcal{N}_{G}(v) denote the neighbourhood of vv, given by the set of adjacent vertices. By P=(p1,…,pk)P=(p_{1},\dots,p_{k}) we denote a path of length k−1k-1 in GG, where p1,…,pkp_{1},\dots,p_{k} are pairwise distinct but adjacent vertices of GG. A tree consisting of a path is called a path tree. For further graph theoretic basics, we refer to [5].

We now introduce the cells of the network realignment complex. A 1-dimensional network realignment corresponds to a single leaf slide, whereas a dd-dimensional network realignment is defined by a collection of dd parallel leaf slides. Note that the concepts formalised in this section generalise the definitions provided in [16] where the base graph is always given by the complete graph G=KnG=K_{n}.

A network realignment N=(T,r)N=(T,r) over GG consists of a partition of the vertices V⁡(G)=A∪BV(G)=A\cup B with |A|≥2|A|\geq 2 such that

    TT is a subtree of GG with vertex set AA,

We call the vertices of TT the specified vertices of NN, and the elements of BB the unspecified vertices of NN.

As an example, consider the complete graph on eight vertices with three edges erased, G=K8∖{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)}G=K_{8}\setminus\{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)\}, as base graph and the network realignment in Figure 1 (a), denoted by N1=(T1,r1)N_{1}=(T_{1},r_{1}). We define PGP_{G}, called the poset of network realignments over GG, by the following:

Definition 1.6.

For a connected graph GG, we let XGX_{G} denote the network realignment complex, given by the cubical structure on the geometric realisation |Δ⁡(PG)||\Delta(P_{G})|.

The action of the automorphism group Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) of the base graph GG on GG translates to an action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on the set of spanning trees of GG. This in turn induces an action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on the poset PGP_{G}. The map g​r:g​B→E⁡(g​T)gr\colon gB\to E(gT) is given by g​r​(g​b)=g⁡(r⁡(b))gr(gb)=g(r(b)). By functoriality the action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on PGP_{G} induces an action on XGX_{G}.

In the following, we will not distinguish between a cubical complex and its face poset and use the same notation for both.

2. Equivariant Topology of the Network Realignment Complex

In this section, we investigate the topology of the network realignment complex over a base graph GG in a way that is compatible with the symmetries of GG. The automorphism group Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) acts on XGX_{G} by relabelling each network realignment, and we seek deformation retracts which do not depend on choices of particular vertex labels. This is reflected in the generalised Morse matchings below. Active vertices of a realignment are defined by structural features such as its spine and occupied leaves. Then matched partners are obtained by (co-)specifying all active vertices simultaneously, rather than choosing a preferred labelled vertex. This construction is completely independent of the labelling and yields Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retracts.

The following theorem gives the resulting equivariant homotopy type of XGX_{G}. It shows that, up to an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant deformation retraction, XGX_{G} has at most one non-contractible component, which is a complete graph on the vertices of GG that support star trees in XGX_{G}.

Theorem 2.1.

Let GG be a connected graph on n≥3n\geq 3 vertices, and let 𝒮G={v∈V⁡(G)∣degG⁡(v)=n−1}\mathcal{S}_{G}=\{v\in V(G)\mid\deg_{G}(v)=n-1\}. The action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on GG restricts to an action on 𝒮G\mathcal{S}_{G}, and hence induces an action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on the complete graph K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} with vertex set 𝒮G\mathcal{S}_{G}.

There exists an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant embedding K𝒮G↪XGK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}\hookrightarrow X_{G} and an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction

XG≃K𝒮G⊔DG,X_{G}\simeq K_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}\sqcup D_{G},

where DGD_{G} is a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space. In particular, after forgetting the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-action, the only component of XGX_{G} with possibly non-trivial homotopy is homotopy equivalent to the complete graph K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}. If k=|𝒮G|≥2k=|\mathcal{S}_{G}|\geq 2, then this is a wedge of (k−1)​(k−2)/2(k-1)(k-2)/2 circles.

The proof of this theorem occupies the rest of this section. After developing the necessary framework of equivariant discrete Morse theory for cubical complexes in Section 2.1, we introduce the minimal spine complex YGY_{G}, an equivariant deformation retract of XGX_{G}, in Section 2.2. In Section 2.3 we identify a distinguished connected component of YGY_{G}, the main component MGM_{G}. We determine the topology of MGM_{G} by showing that it Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariantly deformation retracts onto K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}. In Section 2.4 we classify the residual connected components of YGY_{G} and show that they are contractible. Finally, in Section 2.5, we illustrate the theory by examining the complexes for several classes of base graphs.

2.1. Equivariant Generalised Morse Theory

Constructing large equivariant Morse matchings is often difficult. Indeed, if there exists a group element that fixes a maximal cell τ\tau while permuting all of its facets, then τ\tau must be critical. In the setting of network realignments, the Morse matching given in [16] requires a choice of an active vertex by its label to determine the matched partner. Such a choice is generally incompatible with equivariance.

Generalised Morse theory circumvents this issue by allowing a cell τ\tau to be matched with any face σ\sigma that is preserved whenever τ\tau is preserved. Since we do not distinguish between the cubical complex XX and its poset, the interval is given by [σ,τ]={α∈X∣σ≤α≤τ}[\sigma,\tau]=\{\alpha\in X\mid\sigma\leq\alpha\leq\tau\}. A matched interval [σ,τ][\sigma,\tau] then deformation retracts onto the part of ∂τ\partial\tau not containing σ\sigma. In the setting of network realignments, this amounts to simultaneously specifying (respectively cospecifying) all active vertices to determine the matched partner. Consequently, no active vertex needs to be chosen.

Freij introduced this equivariant generalisation of discrete Morse theory [8]. We adapt his results for our purposes. First, simplicial complexes are replaced by cubical complexes. Further, we restrict to generalised Morse matchings whose critical cells form a subcomplex. This yields the stronger result that the subcomplex of critical cells is a Λ\Lambda-equivariant deformation retract. The proof of this result is given in Appendix A.

Definition 2.2.

Let XX be a cubical Λ\Lambda-complex, and let ∼\sim be an equivalence relation on XX whose equivalence classes are intervals in XX. Then ∼\sim is called a generalised Morse matching if there exists no cycle

σ1<τ1>σ2<τ2>…>σk<τk>σk+1=σ1\sigma_{1}<\tau_{1}>\sigma_{2}<\tau_{2}>\ldots>\sigma_{k}<\tau_{k}>\sigma_{k+1}=\sigma_{1}

with k≥2k\geq 2 and σi∼τi≁σi+1\sigma_{i}\sim\tau_{i}\nsim\sigma_{i+1} for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. A cell is called critical if it is alone in its equivalence class under ∼\sim.

Additionally, the matching ∼\sim is called Λ\Lambda-equivariant if, whenever σ∼τ\sigma\sim\tau, it follows that g​σ∼g​τg\sigma\sim g\tau for all g∈Λg\in\Lambda.

Theorem 2.3.

Let ∼\sim be a Λ\Lambda-equivariant generalised Morse matching on a finite cubical Λ\Lambda-complex XX. Assume that the critical cells of ∼\sim form a subcomplex UU. Then the subcomplex UU is a Λ\Lambda-equivariant strong deformation retract of XX.

2.2. Collapse onto the Minimal Spine Complex YGY_{G}

The goal of this section is to construct a perfect, Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant generalised Morse matching on XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}, where YGY_{G} denotes the subcomplex that consists of the network realignments with minimal spines. Consequently, YGY_{G} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of XGX_{G}.

The central tool for defining this matching is the spine of a network realignment. It was first defined in [16].

Definition 2.4.

Let N=(T,r)N=(T,r) be a network realignment over GG. The spine of NN, denoted by Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N), is the subtree of TT consisting of Int⁡(T)\Int(T) and Im⁡(r)\Image(r). The size of the spine |Sp⁡(N)||\Sp(N)| is the number of the edges of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N).

Similar to the matching given in [16], the matching we construct in this subsection is designed to reduce the size of the spine. For example, given a vertex in XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}, we match it to the coface obtained by cospecifying all leaves whose parent is a leaf of the spine to the corresponding leaf edge of the spine. This coface lies in XGX_{G} if and only if each of the cospecifications is well-defined over the base graph GG.

The obstruction arises from edges missing in GG, which prevent leaves from being slid freely along the underlying tree. For example, the vertex 2 restricts the possible slides of the leaf 1 in any network realignment over G=K8∖{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)}G=K_{8}\setminus\{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)\}. Figure 3 (a) shows a network realignment over GG. As pT​(1)=7p_{T}(1)=7, the vertex 1 cannot be realigned to the vertex 6, since the network realignment in (b) is not a network realignment over GG. The red dotted lines depict all of the connections that are not permitted for network realignments over GG.

Definition 2.5.

Let v,w∈V⁡(G)v,w\in V(G). Then vv is called a barrier of ww if (v,w)∉E⁡(G)(v,w)\notin E(G).

This obstruction is particularly interesting if a leaf vv is attached to a leaf uu of the spine and cannot be slid into the interior of the spine, since pSp⁡(N)​(u)p_{\Sp(N)}(u) is a barrier of vv. In this case, any sequence of realignments not involving pSp⁡(N)​(u)p_{\Sp(N)}(u) preserves the property that the unique path from vv to pSp⁡(N)​(u)p_{\Sp(N)}(u) passes through uu. Therefore, uu remains an interior vertex of the resulting network and, in particular, stays in the spine.

Definition 2.6.

Let NN be a network realignment over GG. A leaf uu of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is called occupied if there exists a vertex v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N)) such that pT​(v)=up_{T}(v)=u and pSp⁡(N)​(u)p_{\Sp(N)}(u) is a barrier of vv. In this situation, we say that vv occupies uu. If no such vertex exists, we say that uu is unoccupied.

Given any two occupied leaves, then both must remain interior vertices, and thus the unique path between them remains in the interior. This provides a lower bound on the spine under any sequence of realignments. In Figure 3 (c), there are two occupied leaves, namely 6 and 8. Every realignment sequence must keep the path between them in the spine. Moreover, if all leaves of the spine are occupied, no sequence of realignments can reduce the size of the spine.

Definition 2.7.

The spine Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) of a network realignment N=(T,r)N=(T,r) is called minimal if |Sp⁡(N)|≤1|\Sp(N)|\leq 1 or all leaves are occupied. We denote by YGY_{G} the subset of XGX_{G} consisting of all network realignments with minimal spines.

As we will see in 2.10, the subset YGY_{G} is a subcomplex of XGX_{G}. To prove this we need the following lemmas.

Lemma 2.8.

If Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{b\to u}), then the sets of occupied leaves of the spines coincide.

Proof.

A vertex v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N)) occupies a leaf of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) if and only if it occupies the same leaf of Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}), since T=Tb→u∖{b}T=T^{b\to u}\setminus\{b\}. Moreover, if u=pTb→u​(b)u=p_{T^{b\to u}}(b) is a leaf of the spine, then bb does not occupy uu in Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}), because pSp⁡(N)​(u)∈r​(b)p_{\Sp(N)}(u)\in r(b), and thus (b,pSp⁡(N)​(u))∈E⁡(G)(b,p_{\Sp(N)}(u))\in E(G), meaning that pSp⁡(N)​(u)p_{\Sp(N)}(u) is not a barrier of bb. Hence, the occupied leaves coincide. ∎

Lemma 2.9.

Let N=(T,r)N=(T,r) be a network realignment over GG. Then Sp⁡(Nb→u)⊆Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{b\to u})\subseteq\Sp(N) for all legal choices b,ub,u.

Proof.

Since G⊆KnG\subseteq K_{n}, NN is a network realignment over KnK_{n}, and the claim was proved for network realignments over KnK_{n} in [16, Proposition 4.7]. ∎

Lemma 2.10.

YGY_{G} is a subcomplex of XGX_{G}.

Proof.

If all leaves of the spine are occupied, then Sp⁡(N)=Int⁡(T)\Sp(N)=\Int(T). Indeed, in this situation every leaf uu of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) lies in Int⁡(T)\Int(T), because there exists a vertex v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N)) with pT​(v)=up_{T}(v)=u, implying degT⁡(u)≥2\degree_{T}(u)\geq 2. Since Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is a subtree of TT, all interior vertices of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) are also interior vertices of TT. This shows the claim if |Sp⁡(N)|≥1|\Sp(N)|\geq 1. If Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is a single vertex, then B=∅B=\emptyset, and again Sp⁡(N)=Int⁡(T)\Sp(N)=\Int(T).

It suffices to prove that N∈YGN\in Y_{G} implies Nb→u∈YGN^{b\to u}\in Y_{G} for all legal choices of vertices b,ub,u. If |Sp⁡(N)|≤1|\Sp(N)|\leq 1, then |Sp⁡(Nb→u)|≤1|\Sp(N^{b\to u})|\leq 1, since Sp⁡(Nb→u)⊆Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{b\to u})\subseteq\Sp(N) by 2.9. If all leaves of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) are occupied, then

Sp⁡(Nb→u)⊆Sp⁡(N)=Int⁡(T)⊆Int⁡(Tb→u)⊆Sp⁡(Nb→u),\Sp(N^{b\to u})\subseteq\Sp(N)=\Int(T)\subseteq\Int(T^{b\to u})\subseteq\Sp(N^{b\to u}),

and thus Sp⁡(Nb→u)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{b\to u})=\Sp(N). By 2.8, the sets of occupied leaves coincide. Thus, all leaves of Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}) are occupied and Nb→u∈YGN^{b\to u}\in Y_{G}. ∎

Definition 2.11.

The set YGY_{G} is called the minimal spine complex of XGX_{G}.

As an example, consider Figure 4, where the base graph is again G=K8∖{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)}G=K_{8}\setminus\{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)\}. The spines are depicted in green. In (a), all leaves of the spine of the network realignment N1N_{1}, namely 6 and 8, are occupied, hence the spine is minimal and N1∈YGN_{1}\in Y_{G}. On the other hand, in (b) the leaf 4 of the spine of the network realignment N2N_{2} is unoccupied. Hence, the spine is not minimal and N2N_{2} is not in YGY_{G}.

Moreover, N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} are connected in XGX_{G} by a sequence of (co-)specifications of the vertex 3. In what follows, we will define an equivalence that matches realignments such as N2N_{2}, leaving only cells with minimal spines, such as N1N_{1}. We will then prove the equivalence relation to be an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant generalised Morse matching.

We define the set of active vertices of a network realignment N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. The following is an adaptation of [16, Definition 4.13] to the present restricted network realignment complex, taking into account the occupied leaves.

Definition 2.12.

Let N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G} be a network realignment over GG. We define

  • •

    ActY+(N)={v∈B∣r(v)=(u,w),u an unoccupied leaf of Sp(N)}\Act_{Y}^{+}(N)=\{v\in B\mid r(v)=(u,w),\>u\text{ an unoccupied leaf of }\Sp(N)\},

  • •

    ActY−(N)={v∈A∣v a leaf of T,pT(v) an unoccupied leaf of Sp(N)}\Act_{Y}^{-}(N)=\{v\in A\mid v\text{ a leaf of }T,\>p_{T}(v)\text{ an unoccupied leaf of }\Sp(N)\},

and ActY⁡(N)=ActY+⁡(N)∪ActY−⁡(N)\Act_{Y}(N)=\Act_{Y}^{+}(N)\cup\Act_{Y}^{-}(N), the set of active vertices.

Lemma 2.13.

If Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is not minimal, then ActY⁡(N)≠∅\Act_{Y}(N)\neq\emptyset.

Proof.

Since Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is not minimal, |Sp⁡(N)|≥2|\Sp(N)|\geq 2 and there exists a leaf uu of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) that is not occupied. Set w=pSp⁡(N)​(u)w=p_{\Sp(N)}(u). If (u,w)∈Im⁡(r)(u,w)\in\Image(r), then ActY+⁡(N)≠∅\Act_{Y}^{+}(N)\neq~\emptyset. On the other hand, if (u,w)∉Im⁡(r)(u,w)\notin\Image(r), then there exists a vertex v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N)) with pT​(v)=up_{T}(v)=u. Since uu is not occupied, v∈ActY−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{-}(N). In both cases, ActY⁡(N)≠∅\Act_{Y}(N)\neq~\emptyset. ∎

Lemma 2.14.

Let N=(T,r)∈XG∖YGN=(T,r)\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. Suppose that N′N^{\prime} is obtained by

  • •

    a specification N′=Nb→uN^{\prime}=N^{b\to u}, where b∈ActY+⁡(N)b\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N) and uu is a leaf of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N), or

  • •

    a cospecification N′=Nv→eN^{\prime}=N^{v\to e}, where v∈ActY−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{-}(N) and e=(pT​(v),pSp⁡(N)​(pT​(v)))e=(p_{T}(v),p_{\Sp(N)}(p_{T}(v))).

Then Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(N′)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{\prime}) and ActY⁡(N)=ActY⁡(N′)\Act_{Y}(N)=\Act_{Y}(N^{\prime}).

Proof.

By 1.7, XGX_{G} is a subcomplex of Xn=XKnX_{n}=X_{K_{n}}. Furthermore, the definition of the set of active vertices given in the present work differs from the one given in [16] only by those vertices whose parent, respectively parent of their specification, is an occupied leaf of the spine. Hence, the proof that the spines of NN and N′N^{\prime} are identical follows from the argument given in [16, Lemma 4.18]. Now, 2.8 implies that the sets of occupied leaves of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) and Sp⁡(N′)\Sp(N^{\prime}) coincide, and consequently, the arguments used in [16, Lemma 4.18] prove the claim. ∎

The previous lemma implies that (co-)specifying all of the active vertices at once will result in network realignments with the same spines and active vertices.

In order to define the partition of cells into intervals for the generalised Morse matching, we first define maps dYd_{Y} and uYu_{Y} on the non-critical cells such that, for each NN, the interval in the partition containing NN is [dY​(N),uY​(N)][d_{Y}(N),u_{Y}(N)].

Definition 2.15.

We define the two maps dY,uY:XG∖YG→XG∖YGd_{Y},u_{Y}\colon X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}\rightarrow X_{G}\setminus Y_{G} as follows. For N=(T,r)∈XG∖YGN=(T,r)\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}, let r⁡(v)=(uv,wv)r(v)=(u_{v},w_{v}) for each v∈ActY+⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N), where uvu_{v} is a leaf of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N). Then the network realignment dY​(N)=(dY​(T),dY​(r))d_{Y}(N)=(d_{Y}(T),d_{Y}(r)) is given by the data

  • •

    dY​(A)=A∪ActY+⁡(N)d_{Y}(A)=A\cup\Act_{Y}^{+}(N),   dY​(B)=B∖ActY+⁡(N)d_{Y}(B)=B\setminus\Act_{Y}^{+}(N),

  • •

    dY​(T)=T∪⋃v∈ActY+⁡(N)(v,uv)d_{Y}(T)=T\cup\bigcup\limits_{v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N)}(v,u_{v}),

  • •

    dY​(r)=r|dY​(B)d_{Y}(r)=r|_{d_{Y}(B)},

and the network realignment uY​(N)=(uY​(T),uY​(r))u_{Y}(N)=(u_{Y}(T),u_{Y}(r)) is defined by the data

  • •

    uY​(A)=A∖ActY−⁡(N)u_{Y}(A)=A\setminus\Act_{Y}^{-}(N),   uY​(B)=B∪ActY−⁡(N)u_{Y}(B)=B\cup\Act_{Y}^{-}(N),

  • •

    uY​(T)=T∖ActY−⁡(N)u_{Y}(T)=T\setminus\Act_{Y}^{-}(N),

  • •

    uY​(r)|B=ru_{Y}(r)|_{B}=r and uY​(r)​(v)=(pT​(v),pSp⁡(N)​(pT​(v)))u_{Y}(r)(v)=(p_{T}(v),p_{\Sp(N)}(p_{T}(v))) for all v∈ActY−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{-}(N).

The network realignment dY​(N)d_{Y}(N) is obtained by specifying every vertex in the set ActY+⁡(N)\Act_{Y}^{+}(N) simultaneously. Accordingly, the network realignment uY​(N)u_{Y}(N) is obtained by cospecifying every vertex in the set ActY−⁡(N)\Act_{Y}^{-}(N) simultaneously. This implies that dY​(N)d_{Y}(N) is a face of NN and uY​(N)u_{Y}(N) is a coface. In conclusion, we have dY​(N)≤N≤uY​(N)d_{Y}(N)\leq N\leq u_{Y}(N). We now define the equivalence relation in the following way.

Definition 2.16.

Let ∼\sim be the collection of intervals in XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G} of the form

[dY​(N),uY​(N)][d_{Y}(N),u_{Y}(N)]

for N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}.

Lemma 2.17.

The collection ∼\sim is a partition of XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. In particular, for a network realignment N~∈XG∖YG\tilde{N}\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}, we have

(2.1) N∈[dY​(N~),uY​(N~)]⇒dY​(N)=dY​(N~)​ and ​uY​(N)=uY​(N~).N\in[d_{Y}(\tilde{N}),u_{Y}(\tilde{N})]\Rightarrow d_{Y}(N)=d_{Y}(\tilde{N})\text{ and }u_{Y}(N)=u_{Y}(\tilde{N}).
Proof.

First, we note that the intervals in ∼\sim really cover the whole set XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. This follows from the existence of an interval [dY​(N),uY​(N)][d_{Y}(N),u_{Y}(N)] for each N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. Next, we turn to the implication (2.1).

Since N∈[dY​(N~),uY​(N~)]N\in[d_{Y}(\tilde{N}),u_{Y}(\tilde{N})], we have

(2.2) dY​(N~)≤N≤uY​(N~).d_{Y}(\tilde{N})\leq N\leq u_{Y}(\tilde{N}).

By definition, uY​(N~)u_{Y}(\tilde{N}) is obtained from dY​(N~)d_{Y}(\tilde{N}) by cospecifying every active vertex. Hence, by (2.2), NN must be obtained from dY​(N~)d_{Y}(\tilde{N}) by cospecifying a subset 𝒜⊆ActY⁡(N~)\mathcal{A}\subseteq\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}) to the corresponding leaf edge of the spine. By iterating 2.14, it follows that ActY⁡(N)=ActY⁡(dY​(N~))\Act_{Y}(N)=\Act_{Y}(d_{Y}(\tilde{N})). This implies conversely that d⁡(N~)d(\tilde{N}) is obtained from NN by specifying every vertex in 𝒜=ActY+⁡(N)\mathcal{A}=\Act_{Y}^{+}(N) to the corresponding leaf of the spine, and hence dY​(N)=dY​(N~)d_{Y}(N)=d_{Y}(\tilde{N}).

On the other hand, NN is obtained from uY​(N~)u_{Y}(\tilde{N}) by specifying a subset of ActY⁡(N~)\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}). Similar arguments lead to uY​(N)=uY​(N~)u_{Y}(N)=u_{Y}(\tilde{N}), and hence the implication of (2.1) is proved.

This implies that the intervals of ∼\sim are disjoint, which means that ∼\sim is a partition. ∎

Lemma 2.18.

Let II be an interval in ∼\sim and N,N~∈IN,\tilde{N}\in I. We have Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(N~)\Sp(N)=\Sp(\tilde{N}) and ActY⁡(N)=ActY⁡(N~)\Act_{Y}(N)=\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}).

Proof.

As in the proof 2.17, applying 2.14 iteratively yields the claim. ∎

Lemma 2.19.

Let NN be a network realignment over GG that is not minimal. If Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{b\to u}), then ActY⁡(Nb→u)⊆ActY⁡(N)\Act_{Y}(N^{b\to u})\subseteq\Act_{Y}(N).

Proof.

The following arguments are similar to the proof of [16, Lemma 4.20], but we have to take into account the relation to the occupied leaves in the set of potential active vertices.

Let v∈ActY⁡(Nb→u)v\in\Act_{Y}(N^{b\to u}). We show that v∈ActY⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}(N). If v∈ActY+⁡(Nb→u)v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N^{b\to u}), then r⁡(v)r(v) is a leaf edge in Sp⁡(Nb→u)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{b\to u})=\Sp(N). Since v∈ActY+⁡(Nb→u)v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N^{b\to u}), both incident vertices to r⁡(v)r(v) are unoccupied in Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}), and thus also unoccupied in Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) by 2.8. Hence, v∈ActY+⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N).

Now, assume v∈ActY−⁡(Nb→u)v\in\Act_{Y}^{-}(N^{b\to u}). If v=bv=b, then uu is a leaf of Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}) and r⁡(b)r(b) is a leaf edge of Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{b\to u}). Then pTb→u​(b)=up_{T^{b\to u}}(b)=u is unoccupied in Nb→uN^{b\to u}, and thus also unoccupied in NN by 2.8. Hence, b∈ActY+⁡(N)b\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N).

If v≠bv\neq b, then vv is a leaf of TT, which is a subtree of Tb→uT^{b\to u}, and pTb→u​(v)=pT​(v)p_{T^{b\to u}}(v)=p_{T}(v) is a leaf of Sp⁡(Nb→u)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{b\to u})=\Sp(N). Since pT​(v)p_{T}(v) is not occupied in Nb→uN^{b\to u}, and thus also unoccupied in Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) by 2.8, we have v∈ActY−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{Y}^{-}(N). ∎

This leads us to the main result.

Proposition 2.20.

The equivalence relation ∼\sim is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant generalised Morse matching on XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}.

Proof.

Assume for a contradiction the existence of a cycle in XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G} of the form

(2.3) N~1<N1>N~2<N2>⋯<Nk>N~1,\tilde{N}_{1}<N_{1}>\tilde{N}_{2}<N_{2}>\cdots<N_{k}>\tilde{N}_{1},

where k≥2k\geq 2, N~i∼Ni\tilde{N}_{i}\sim N_{i}, and NiN_{i} and N~i+1\tilde{N}_{i+1} belong to distinct equivalence classes for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. For convenience, we set N~k+1=N~1\tilde{N}_{k+1}=\tilde{N}_{1}.

By 2.9 and 2.18, all cells appearing in (2.3) have the same spine, i.e. Sp⁡(N~)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(\tilde{N})=\Sp(N) for all N~,N∈{N~1,…,N~k,N1,…,Nk}\tilde{N},N\in\{\tilde{N}_{1},\dots,\tilde{N}_{k},N_{1},\dots,N_{k}\}. Furthermore, 2.18 and 2.19 imply ActY⁡(N~)=ActY⁡(N)\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N})=\Act_{Y}(N).

The relation Ni>N~i+1N_{i}>\tilde{N}_{i+1} means that N~i+1\tilde{N}_{i+1} is obtained from NiN_{i} by specifying a non-empty subset of vertices in BB of NiN_{i}, not all of which are active and specified to the leaf of the spine. Thus one of the following occurs.

  • (a)

    A vertex v∈ActY+⁡(Ni)v\in\Act_{Y}^{+}(N_{i}) is specified such that N~i+1≁Ni\tilde{N}_{i+1}\not\sim N_{i}. Hence, vv is attached to an interior vertex of the spine. However, since Sp⁡(N~i+1)=Sp⁡(Ni)\Sp(\tilde{N}_{i+1})=\Sp(N_{i}), it follows that v∉ActY⁡(N~i+1)v\notin\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}), contradicting ActY⁡(Ni)=ActY⁡(N~i+1)\Act_{Y}(N_{i})=\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}).

  • (b)

    A vertex v∉ActY⁡(Ni)v\notin\Act_{Y}(N_{i}), v∈Bv\in B is specified. Since v∉ActY⁡(N~i)v\notin\Act_{Y}(\tilde{N}_{i}), it can never be cospecified later. Consequently, the sequence |B∖ActY||B\setminus\Act_{Y}| decreases along the cycle, preventing a return to N~1\tilde{N}_{1}.

To conclude, this contradicts the existence of the cycle (2.3). Hence, ∼\sim is a generalised Morse matching.

By 2.13, every N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G} satisfies ActY⁡(N)≠∅\Act_{Y}(N)\neq\emptyset, and therefore dY​(N)≠uY​(N)d_{Y}(N)\neq u_{Y}(N). Thus, no interval of ∼\sim consists of a single cell, and the critical cells are precisely those of YGY_{G}. Moreover, 2.17 implies that the matching is well-defined.

Finally, it is easy to see that any automorphism gg of GG preserves the spine: g​Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(g​N)g\Sp(N)=\Sp(gN). Furthermore, since the adjacency of Kn∖GK_{n}\setminus G is preserved, gg maps occupied leaves to occupied leaves and this implies g​Act+⁡(N)=Act+⁡(g​N)g\Act^{+}(N)=\Act^{+}(gN) as well as g​Act−⁡(N)=Act−⁡(g​N)g\Act^{-}(N)=\Act^{-}(gN). Hence, g​dY​(N)=dY​(g​N)gd_{Y}(N)=d_{Y}(gN) and g​uY​(N)=uY​(g​N)gu_{Y}(N)=u_{Y}(gN). Consequently,

[g​dY​(N),g​uY​(N)]=[dY​(g​N),uY​(g​N)][gd_{Y}(N),gu_{Y}(N)]=[d_{Y}(gN),u_{Y}(gN)]

is matched in ∼\sim for any N∈XG∖YGN\in X_{G}\setminus Y_{G}. It follows that ∼\sim is Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant. ∎

Proposition 2.21.

The minimal spine complex YGY_{G} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of XGX_{G}.

Proof.

By 2.20, we know that ∼\sim is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant generalised Morse matching whose set of critical cells YGY_{G} is a subcomplex of XGX_{G} by 2.10. Consequently, Theorem 2.3 gives the strong deformation retraction. ∎

2.3. The Main Component of YGY_{G}

As discussed earlier, the path between any two occupied leaves remains contained in the spine under any sequence of network realignments over GG. Conversely, if a network realignment with minimal spine has precisely one occupied leaf, then every vertex can be slid to that occupied leaf. The resulting network realignment is a star tree of GG.

We split the analysis of the topology of YGY_{G} into two parts. We begin with the main component MGM_{G}, which contains all the star trees of GG and is the only connected component that is not necessarily contractible. To show that MGM_{G} Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariantly retracts onto K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}, the complete graph whose vertices are the star trees of GG, we first construct a further generalised Morse matching that collapses all network realignments with a single occupied leaf to the star tree with the occupied leaf as interior vertex. The resulting subcomplex contains precisely the star trees and the (n−2)(n-2)-cubes connecting them. K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} is a strong deformation retract of this subcomplex.

Definition 2.22.

Let MG⊆YGM_{G}\subseteq Y_{G} consist of all cells NN of YGY_{G} whose spine has at most one occupied vertex in Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N). We call MGM_{G} the main component of YGY_{G}.

Note that N∈MGN\in M_{G} implies |Sp⁡(N)|≤1|\Sp(N)|\leq 1. Let NN be a network realignment with |Sp⁡(N)|≥2|\Sp(N)|\geq 2. Then its spine contains at least two leaves. Thus, if N∈YGN\in Y_{G}, the spine would have at least two occupied vertices, and hence N∉MGN\notin M_{G}.

Associated to each star tree sis_{i} of GG is a vertex of MGM_{G}, which we will also denote by sis_{i}. Clearly, the star tree with center vertex ii is a tree of GG if and only if degG⁡(i)=n−1\deg_{G}(i)=n-1. The star trees are precisely the vertices of XGX_{G} whose spine has size 00.

Proposition 2.23.

MGM_{G} is a connected component of YGY_{G}. Moreover, MGM_{G} is preserved by the action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G).

Proof.

We start by showing that MGM_{G} is a subcomplex of YGY_{G}. Let N∈MGN\in M_{G}. If |Sp⁡(N)|=0|\Sp(N)|=0, then B=∅B=\emptyset and TT is a star tree. If |Sp⁡(N)|=1|\Sp(N)|=1, then either |Sp⁡(Nb→u)|=0|\Sp(N^{b\to u})|=0, and thus Nb→u∈MGN^{b\to u}\in M_{G}, or Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{b\to u}). Then, by 2.8, the occupied leaves of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) and Sp⁡(Nb→u)\Sp(N^{b\to u}) coincide, and again Nb→u∈MGN^{b\to u}\in M_{G}. Therefore, MGM_{G} is a subcomplex of YGY_{G}.

To show that MGM_{G} is connected, we show that any two vertices of MGM_{G} are connected. Let N0=(T0,r0)∈MGN_{0}=(T_{0},r_{0})\in M_{G} be 0-dimensional with |Sp⁡(N0)|=1|\Sp(N_{0})|=1. Choose uu to be the unoccupied vertex of Sp⁡(N0)\Sp(N_{0}), and let ww denote the other vertex. Let w,v1,…,vkw,v_{1},\ldots,v_{k} denote the neighbours of uu in T0T_{0}. Define Ni=(Ni−1vi→(u,w))vi→wN_{i}=(N_{i-1}^{v_{i}\to(u,w)})^{v_{i}\to w} for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, and consider the path

N0,N1,…,Nk−1,NkN_{0},N_{1},\ldots,N_{k-1},N_{k}

in YGY_{G}. We have

Sp⁡(N0)=Sp⁡(N0v1→(u,w))=…=Sp⁡(Nk−1)=Sp⁡(Nk−1vk→(u,w)),\Sp(N_{0})=\Sp(N_{0}^{v_{1}\to(u,w)})=\ldots=\Sp(N_{k-1})=\Sp(N_{k-1}^{v_{k}\to(u,w)}),

and V⁡(Sp⁡(Nk))={w}V(\Sp(N_{k}))=\{w\}. By 2.8, all network realignments of this sequence are contained in MGM_{G}. Thus, any 0-dimensional cell in MGM_{G} is connected to a star tree. Clearly, any two star trees sis_{i} and sjs_{j} that are contained in YGY_{G} are connected by the (n−2)(n-2)-cubes. Therefore, MGM_{G} is connected.

To conclude the proof that MGM_{G} is a connected component, it is enough to show that if N∈MGN\in M_{G}, then Nv→e∈YGN^{v\to e}\in Y_{G} implies Nv→e∈MGN^{v\to e}\in M_{G}. Given N∈MGN\in M_{G} and Nv→e∈YGN^{v\to e}\in Y_{G}, we write e=(u,w)e=(u,w) with pT​(v)=up_{T}(v)=u. If |Sp⁡(N)|=0|\Sp(N)|=0, then |Sp⁡(Nv→e)|=1|\Sp(N^{v\to e})|=1. Since degTv→e⁡(w)=degT⁡(w)=1\degree_{T^{v\to e}}(w)=\degree_{T}(w)=1, it follows that ww is not occupied in Sp⁡(Nv→e)\Sp(N^{v\to e}). Hence, Sp⁡(Nv→e)\Sp(N^{v\to e}) has at most one occupied vertex and is contained in MGM_{G}. On the other hand, assume that |Sp⁡(N)|=1|\Sp(N)|=1. If Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nv→e)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{v\to e}), then the occupied leaves coincide by 2.8. Therefore, N∈MGN\in M_{G} directly implies Nv→e∈MGN^{v\to e}\in M_{G}. Otherwise, |Sp⁡(Nv→e)|=2|\Sp(N^{v\to e})|=2. We observe that 𝒩Tv→e​(w)=𝒩T​(w)={u}\mathcal{N}_{T^{v\to e}}(w)=\mathcal{N}_{T}(w)=\{u\}, and thus ww is not occupied in Sp⁡(Nv→e)\Sp(N^{v\to e}) and Nv→e∉YGN^{v\to e}\notin Y_{G}.

It remains to show that g​MG=MGgM_{G}=M_{G} for all g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G). Since the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-action is induced by permuting the vertices of each network realignment, it preserves the isomorphism type of the underlying tree. In particular, star trees are mapped to star trees. As MGM_{G} is a connected component containing all star trees of GG, it follows that g​MG=MGgM_{G}=M_{G}. ∎

Our goal is to retract MGM_{G} onto the subcomplex ΣG\Sigma_{G}, which contains the following types of cells. Let sis_{i} and sjs_{j} correspond to two star trees of GG. Both are faces of the (n−2)(n-2)-dimensional cell indexed by the network realignment N=(T,r)N=(T,r), where A={i,j},B=V⁡(G)∖{i,j}A=\{i,j\},\>B=V(G)\setminus\{i,j\}, and rr is the constant map with value (i,j)(i,j). Let Ci,jC_{i,j} denote the subcomplex of MGM_{G} containing NN and all of its specifications. Ci,jC_{i,j} is isomorphic to an (n−2)(n-2)-cube. For the preceding, we also refer to [16, Proposition 4.9].

Definition 2.24.

Let 𝒮G={v∈V⁡(G)∣degG⁡(v)=n−1}\mathcal{S}_{G}=\{v\in V(G)\mid\degree_{G}(v)=n-1\} be the set of vertices of GG that determine the star trees in XGX_{G}. If |𝒮G|≥2|\mathcal{S}_{G}|\geq 2, we define the subcomplex

ΣG=⋃i≠j∈𝒮GCi,j.\Sigma_{G}=\bigcup_{i\neq j\in\mathcal{S}_{G}}C_{i,j}.

If 𝒮G={i}\mathcal{S}_{G}=\{i\}, then we define ΣG={si}\Sigma_{G}=\{s_{i}\} and, if 𝒮G=∅\mathcal{S}_{G}=\emptyset, we define ΣG=∅\Sigma_{G}=\emptyset.

ΣG\Sigma_{G} is a subcomplex, since it is the union of the cubes Ci,jC_{i,j}. Moreover, ΣG\Sigma_{G} is Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-invariant, as it consists precisely of the (n−2)(n-2)-cubes of XGX_{G}. Finally, if N∈Ci,jN\in C_{i,j}, then V⁡(Sp⁡(N))⊆{i,j}⊆𝒮GV(\Sp(N))\subseteq\{i,j\}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{G}, so every vertex of Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N) is unoccupied. Therefore, ΣG\Sigma_{G} is contained in MGM_{G}.

To determine the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant topology of the main component, we first show that ΣG\Sigma_{G} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of MGM_{G}. For this, we introduce another generalised Morse matching.

Notice that a network realignment belongs to ΣG\Sigma_{G} if and only if its spine consists either of a single point or of a single edge with none of its leaves occupied. In particular, the network realignments in MG∖ΣGM_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} are those whose spine is a single edge with exactly one occupied vertex. An example of this is illustrated in Figure 5 (a).

Definition 2.25.

Let N∈MG∖ΣGN\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} be a network realignment. We denote its spine by (uN,wN)(u_{N},w_{N}), where uNu_{N} is the unique occupied vertex. We define

  • •

    ActM+⁡(N)=B\Act_{M}^{+}(N)=B,

  • •

    ActM−⁡(N)=𝒩T​(wN)∖{uN}\Act_{M}^{-}(N)=\mathcal{N}_{T}(w_{N})\setminus\{u_{N}\}  and

  • •

    ActM⁡(N)=ActM+⁡(N)∪ActM−⁡(N)\Act_{M}(N)=\Act_{M}^{+}(N)\cup\Act_{M}^{-}(N).

The vertices in ActM⁡(N)\Act_{M}(N) are called active vertices.

We observe that the vertices which are not active are exactly uNu_{N} together with its neighbourhood, precisely:

(2.4) 𝒩T​(uN)=V⁡(G)∖{ActM⁡(N)∪uN}.\mathcal{N}_{T}(u_{N})=V(G)\setminus\{\Act_{M}(N)\cup u_{N}\}.

The cardinality of the set of active vertices is a measure of the distance to the star tree suNs_{u_{N}}.

Lemma 2.26.

Any network realignment N∈MG∖ΣGN\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} has at least one active vertex. Moreover, NN is uniquely determined by its spine, ActM+⁡(N)\Act_{M}^{+}(N) and ActM−⁡(N)\Act_{M}^{-}(N).

Proof.

Suppose that NN has no active vertices. ActM+⁡(N)=∅\Act_{M}^{+}(N)=\emptyset means that NN is a 0-dimensional realignment. It follows from ActM−⁡(N)=∅\Act_{M}^{-}(N)=\emptyset and N∈MGN\in M_{G} that NN is a star tree. But then NN lies in ΣG\Sigma_{G}.

Let N1=(T1,r1),N2=(T2,r2)∈MG∖ΣGN_{1}=(T_{1},r_{1}),N_{2}=(T_{2},r_{2})\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} with Sp⁡(N1)=Sp⁡(N2),ActM+⁡(N1)=ActM+⁡(N2)\Sp(N_{1})=\Sp(N_{2}),\>\Act_{M}^{+}(N_{1})=\Act_{M}^{+}(N_{2}), and ActM−⁡(N1)=ActM−⁡(N2)\Act_{M}^{-}(N_{1})=\Act_{M}^{-}(N_{2}). Since wN1w_{N_{1}} is not occupied, we have (uN1,v)∈E⁡(G)(u_{N_{1}},v)\in E(G) for all v∈𝒩T1​(wN1)∖{uN1}v\in\mathcal{N}_{T_{1}}(w_{N_{1}})\setminus\{u_{N_{1}}\} and any specified vertex of GG not contained in 𝒩T1​(wN1)∖{uN1}\mathcal{N}_{T_{1}}(w_{N_{1}})\setminus\{u_{N_{1}}\} is adjacent to uN1u_{N_{1}} in T1T_{1}. Further, for an unspecified vertex b∈B1b\in B_{1}, we have r1​(b)=(uN1,wN1)r_{1}(b)=(u_{N_{1}},w_{N_{1}}), and thus degG⁡(uN1)=n−1\degree_{G}(u_{N_{1}})=n-1. Similarly for N2N_{2}. Therefore, uN1=uN2u_{N_{1}}=u_{N_{2}} and wN1=wN2w_{N_{1}}=w_{N_{2}}. By definition of the active vertices, it follows that N1=N2N_{1}=N_{2}. ∎

Let N=(T,r)∈MG∖ΣGN=(T,r)\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}, and v∈ActM⁡(N)v\in\Act_{M}(N). Let xx be a leaf of TT that occupies uNu_{N}. If v∈ActM+⁡(N)v\in\Act_{M}^{+}(N), then uNu_{N} is adjacent to wNw_{N} and xx, and wNw_{N} is adjacent to uNu_{N} and vv in Nv→wNN^{v\to w_{N}}, and thus Sp⁡(Nv→wN)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{v\to w_{N}})=\Sp(N). By 2.8, the occupied leaves remain unchanged. Consequently, Nv→wN∈MG∖ΣGN^{v\to w_{N}}\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}. If v∈ActM−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{M}^{-}(N), then again Sp⁡(Nv→(uN,wN))=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N^{v\to(u_{N},w_{N})})=\Sp(N) and Nv→(uN,wN)∈MG∖ΣGN^{v\to(u_{N},w_{N})}\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}.

This motivates the definition of the realignments dM​(N)d_{M}(N) and uM​(N)u_{M}(N), in which all active vertices are specified and cospecified, respectively. This corresponds to 2.15 of the interval limits in XG∖YGX_{G}\setminus Y_{G}.

Definition 2.27.

We define two maps dM,uM:MG∖ΣG→MG∖ΣGd_{M},u_{M}\colon M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}\rightarrow M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}. Let N∈MG∖ΣGN\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}. The network realignment dM​(N)=(dM​(T),dM​(r))d_{M}(N)=(d_{M}(T),d_{M}(r)) is given by

  • •

    dM​(A)=A∪ActM+⁡(N)=V⁡(G),dM​(B)=B∖ActM+⁡(N)=∅d_{M}(A)=A\cup\Act_{M}^{+}(N)=V(G),\quad d_{M}(B)=B\setminus\Act_{M}^{+}(N)=\emptyset,

    dM​(T)=T∪⋃v∈ActM+⁡(N)(v,wN)d_{M}(T)=T\cup\bigcup\limits_{v\in\Act_{M}^{+}(N)}(v,w_{N}),

and the network realignment uM​(N)=(uM​(T),uM​(r))u_{M}(N)=(u_{M}(T),u_{M}(r)) is given by

  • •

    uM​(A)=A∖ActM−⁡(N),uM​(B)=B∪ActM−⁡(N)u_{M}(A)=A\setminus\Act_{M}^{-}(N),\quad u_{M}(B)=B\cup\Act_{M}^{-}(N),

  • •

    uM​(T)=T∖ActM−⁡(N)u_{M}(T)=T\setminus\Act_{M}^{-}(N),

  • •

    uM​(r)​(v)=(uN,wN)u_{M}(r)(v)=(u_{N},w_{N}) for all v∈uM​(B)v\in u_{M}(B).

As an example, consider Figure 5. (a) which shows a network realignment N∈MG∖ΣGN\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}. The unique occupied vertex of the spine is 7, since (4,5)∉E⁡(G)(4,5)\notin E(G) and 7 has degree n−1n-1 in GG. The network realignment dM​(N)d_{M}(N), shown in (b), is given by specifying all vertices in ActM+⁡(N)=B={3,6}\Act_{M}^{+}(N)=B=\{3,6\} to the unoccupied vertex 4, whereas uM​(N)u_{M}(N) is given by cospecifying all vertices in ActM−⁡(N)=𝒩T​(4)∖{7}={2,8}\Act_{M}^{-}(N)=\mathcal{N}_{T}(4)\setminus\{7\}=\{2,8\} to the edge (4,7)(4,7), as depicted in (c).

For each NN, it is clear that dM​(N)d_{M}(N) is a face of NN and uM​(N)u_{M}(N) is a coface. Now, let N,N~∈MG∖ΣGN,\tilde{N}\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} such that dM​(N)≤N~≤uM​(N)d_{M}(N)\leq\tilde{N}\leq u_{M}(N). Then, it holds that 𝒩N~​(uN~)=𝒩N​(uN)\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{N}}(u_{\tilde{N}})=\mathcal{N}_{N}(u_{N}), and by (2.4) equivalently ActM⁡(N~)=ActM⁡(N)\Act_{M}(\tilde{N})=\Act_{M}(N). Further, the spines of every cell in the interval [dM​(N),uM​(N)][d_{M}(N),u_{M}(N)] are identical, since specifying a vertex v∈ActM+⁡(N)v~\in~\Act_{M}^{+}(N) to wNw_{N} and cospecifying a vertex v∈ActM−⁡(N)v\in\Act_{M}^{-}(N) to (uN,wN)(u_{N},w_{N}), respectively, does not change the spine. Using additionally 2.26, we then describe the interval in an explicit way:

[dM(N),uM(N)]={N′∈MG∖ΣG∣Sp(N′)=Sp(N),ActM(N′)=ActM(N)}.[d_{M}(N),u_{M}(N)]=\{N^{\prime}\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}\mid\Sp(N^{\prime})=\Sp(N),\>\Act_{M}(N^{\prime})=\Act_{M}(N)\}.

This also implies that dM​(N~)=dM​(N)d_{M}(\tilde{N})=d_{M}(N) and uM​(N~)=uM​(N)u_{M}(\tilde{N})=u_{M}(N). By the preceding, these intervals give a well-defined partition.

Definition 2.28.

Let ∼\sim be the collection of intervals in MG∖ΣGM_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} of the form

[dM​(N),uM​(N)][d_{M}(N),u_{M}(N)]

for N∈MG∖ΣGN\in M_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G}.

Proposition 2.29.

The collection ∼\sim is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant generalised Morse matching.

Proof.

We show that ∼\sim is a generalised Morse matching. Let

N~1<N1>N~2<N2>…>N~k<Nk>N~k+1=N~1\tilde{N}_{1}<N_{1}>\tilde{N}_{2}<N_{2}>\ldots>\tilde{N}_{k}<N_{k}>\tilde{N}_{k+1}=\tilde{N}_{1}

be a cycle in MG∖ΣGM_{G}\setminus\Sigma_{G} with dM​(N~i)=dM​(Ni)≠dM​(N~i+1)d_{M}(\tilde{N}_{i})=d_{M}(N_{i})\neq d_{M}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}) for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. Because N~i+1<Ni\tilde{N}_{i+1}<N_{i} and |Sp⁡(N~i+1)|=1|\Sp(\tilde{N}_{i+1})|=1, we have Sp⁡(N~i+1)=Sp⁡(Ni)\Sp(\tilde{N}_{i+1})=\Sp(N_{i}). This implies ActM⁡(Ni)≠ActM⁡(N~i+1)\Act_{M}(N_{i})\neq\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}) for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, and uN~i+1=uNiu_{\tilde{N}_{i+1}}=u_{N_{i}}. Hence, combining this with equation (2.4), we find 𝒩Ti​(uNi)⊆𝒩T~i+1​(uN~i+1)\mathcal{N}_{T_{i}}(u_{N_{i}})\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{T}_{i+1}}(u_{\tilde{N}_{i+1}}). It follows

ActM⁡(N~i+1)\displaystyle\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}) =V⁡(G)∖({uN~i+1}∪𝒩T~i+1​(uN~i+1))\displaystyle=V(G)\setminus(\{u_{\tilde{N}_{i+1}}\}\cup\mathcal{N}_{\tilde{T}_{i+1}}(u_{\tilde{N}_{i+1}}))
⊆V⁡(G)∖({uNi}∪𝒩Ti​(uNi))=ActM⁡(Ni).\displaystyle\subseteq V(G)\setminus(\{u_{N_{i}}\}\cup\mathcal{N}_{T_{i}}(u_{N_{i}}))=\Act_{M}(N_{i}).

Therefore, ActM⁡(Ni)⊋ActM⁡(N~i+1)\Act_{M}(N_{i})\supsetneq\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{i+1}) and

ActM⁡(N~1)=ActM⁡(N1)⊋…⊋ActM⁡(N~k)=ActM⁡(Nk)⊋ActM⁡(N~1).\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{1})=\Act_{M}(N_{1})\supsetneq\ldots\supsetneq\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{k})=\Act_{M}(N_{k})\supsetneq\Act_{M}(\tilde{N}_{1}).

Consequently, k=1k=1 and ∼\sim is acyclic.

Finally, the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariance of the generalised Morse matching ∼\sim is given since the construction is independent of the labelling of the vertices. ∎

Proposition 2.30.

ΣG\Sigma_{G} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of MGM_{G}.

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of 2.29 and Theorem 2.3. ∎

It remains to determine the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant homotopy type of ΣG\Sigma_{G}. We extend Corollary 4.10 in [16] to general graphs in an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant setting. For this purpose, we introduce the subcomplex K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}.

Definition 2.31.

Let 𝒮G={v∈V⁡(G)∣deg⁡(v)=n−1}\mathcal{S}_{G}=\{v\in V(G)\mid\deg(v)=n-1\} and let K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} denote the complete graph with vertex set 𝒮G\mathcal{S}_{G}. Since graph automorphisms preserve degrees, the action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on GG restricts to 𝒮G\mathcal{S}_{G} and thus induces an action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) on K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}.

We define an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant topological embedding

ι:K𝒮G↪ΣG\iota\colon K_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}\hookrightarrow\Sigma_{G}

by sending the vertex i∈𝒮Gi\in\mathcal{S}_{G} to the star tree sis_{i} and the edge (i,j)(i,j) to the diagonal di,jd_{i,j} between sis_{i} and sjs_{j} in Ci,j⊆ΣGC_{i,j}\subseteq\Sigma_{G}.

Henceforth, we identify K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} with its image under ι\iota.

Proposition 2.32.

K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of ΣG\Sigma_{G}.

Proof.

For any i≠j∈𝒮Gi\neq j\in\mathcal{S}_{G} the intersection of Ci,jC_{i,j} and the subspace K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} contains precisely the diagonal joining the two opposite vertices sis_{i} and sjs_{j}. We retract Ci,jC_{i,j} onto this diagonal by the straight-line homotopy from each point to its orthogonal projection onto the diagonal. This fixes the diagonal pointwise.

These deformation retractions agree on intersections, because distinct (n−2)(n-2)-cubes meet only in star tree vertices, where the homotopy is constant. Hence the contractions glue to a deformation retraction of ΣG\Sigma_{G} onto K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}.

Any automorphism g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G) sends Ci,jC_{i,j} to Cg​i,g​jC_{gi,gj}, sends the diagonal di,jd_{i,j} to dg​i,g​jd_{gi,gj}, and preserves orthogonal projection to these diagonals. Therefore, the resulting strong deformation retraction is Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant. ∎

Proposition 2.33.

K𝒮GK_{\mathcal{S}_{G}} is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract of MGM_{G}.

Proof.

This follows from 2.32 and 2.30. ∎

2.4. The Residual Components of YGY_{G}

The preceding subsection gives a complete description of the topology of the main component MGM_{G}. Our next goal is to determine the topology of the remaining connected components of YGY_{G}.

Definition 2.34.

By RGR_{G} we denote the complement of MGM_{G} in YGY_{G}. The connected components of RGR_{G} are called residual components.

Since, by 2.23, the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-action on YGY_{G} restricts to the main component, it also restricts to its complement RGR_{G}.

We proceed by classifying the residual components by their spines and spine assignments. We then give a cubical description of the residual components as products of subtrees of their spines. This description is compatible with the action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G) and allows us to contract RGR_{G} equivariantly to a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space.

Definition 2.35.

Let N∈XGN\in X_{G} be a network realignment. Let ZN=V⁡(G)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))Z_{N}=V(G)\setminus V(\Sp(N)). The spine assignment cNc_{N} of NN assigns to every vertex v∈ZNv\in Z_{N} a connected component cN​(v)c_{N}(v) of Sp⁡(N)∖{w∈Sp⁡(N)∣w​ is a barrier of ​v}\Sp(N)\setminus\{w\in\Sp(N)\mid w\text{ is a barrier of }v\} as follows:

  • •

    if v∈Bv\in B, then cN​(v)c_{N}(v) is the component containing r⁡(v)r(v),

  • •

    if v∈Av\in A, then cN​(v)c_{N}(v) is the component containing pT​(v)p_{T}(v).

Example 2.36.

As an example of two different spine assignments, consider Figure 6. Take G=K8∖{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)}G=K_{8}\setminus\{(1,2),(2,3),(4,5)\}. The network realignments depicted in Figure 6 certainly have the same spine. However, since 22 is a barrier of 33, the movement of 33 is restricted to either the left hand side or the right hand side of 22. This condition is expressed by the spine assignment. In (a), the spine assignment assigns to 33 the subtree (7,5,8)(7,5,8) and in (b) it assigns to 33 the single vertex subtree (6)(6). As stated in the following proposition, this means that the two network realignments are contained in different connected components of YGY_{G}.

Proposition 2.37.

Any two network realignments in RGR_{G} lie in the same connected component of RGR_{G} if and only if they have the same spine and the same spine assignment.

Proof.

For N=(T,r)∈RGN=(T,r)\in R_{G}, spine and spine assignments are stable under specification. Suppose V⁡(Sp⁡(N))∖V⁡(Sp⁡(Nb→w))={u}V(\Sp(N))\setminus V(\Sp(N^{b\to w}))=\{u\}. Then r⁡(b)=(u,w)r(b)=(u,w) and degT⁡(u)=1\degree_{T}(u)=1. Hence, uu is not occupied in Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N), contradicting N∈RGN\in R_{G}. It follows that Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(Nb→w)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{b\to w}). Since pT​(v)=pTb→w​(v)p_{T}(v)=p_{T^{b\to w}}(v) if v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N))v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N)) and r​(v)=rb→w​(v)r(v)=r^{b\to w}(v) if v∈B∖{b}v\in B\setminus\{b\}, we have cN​(v)=cNb→w​(v)c_{N}(v)=c_{N^{b\to w}}(v) for all v≠bv\neq b. Because pTb→w​(b)=w∈r⁡(b)p_{T^{b\to w}}(b)=w\in r(b), also cN​(b)=cNb→w​(b)c_{N}(b)=c_{N^{b\to w}}(b). Thus, cN=cNb→wc_{N}=c_{N^{b\to w}}, proving the claim.

It remains to show that N=(T,r)N=(T,r) and N′=(T′,r′)N^{\prime}=(T^{\prime},r^{\prime}) lie within the same connected component if their spine and spine assignments coincide. It suffices to consider 0-dimensional realignments N,N′∈RGN,N^{\prime}\in R_{G} with Sp⁡(N)=Sp⁡(N′)\Sp(N)=\Sp(N^{\prime}) and cN=cN′c_{N}=c_{N^{\prime}}. Consider v∈ZN=ZN′v\in Z_{N}=Z_{N^{\prime}}. Then pT​(v)p_{T}(v) and pT′​(v)p_{T^{\prime}}(v) are contained within the same connected component cN​(v)=cN′​(v)c_{N}(v)=c_{N^{\prime}}(v). Let pT​(v)=u0,u1,…,uk=pT′​(v)p_{T}(v)=u_{0},u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}=p_{T^{\prime}}(v) be the unique path between pT​(v)p_{T}(v) and pT′​(v)p_{T^{\prime}}(v) in Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N). Realigning vv along this path and doing this iteratively for all vertices in ZNZ_{N} yields a sequence of network realignments connecting NN and N′N^{\prime}. ∎

Definition 2.38.

Let Γ\Gamma be a residual component. By 2.37, Sp⁡(N)\Sp(N), ZNZ_{N} and cNc_{N} are independent of the choice of N∈ΓN\in\Gamma. We define Sp⁡(Γ)=Sp⁡(N)\Sp(\Gamma)=\Sp(N), ZΓ=ZNZ_{\Gamma}=Z_{N} and cΓ=cNc_{\Gamma}=c_{N} for any choice of N∈ΓN\in\Gamma.

Lemma 2.39.

The spine and spine assignment respect the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-action in the following sense. Let g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G) and let Γ\Gamma be a connected component of RGR_{G}, then Sp⁡(g​Γ)=g​Sp⁡(Γ)\Sp(g\Gamma)=g\Sp(\Gamma). Let N=(T,r)∈ΓN=(T,r)\in\Gamma and g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G). cg​Γ​(w)=g​cΓ​(v)=g​cΓ​(g−1​w),c_{g\Gamma}(w)=g\,c_{\Gamma}(v)=g\,c_{\Gamma}(g^{-1}w),

which proves the claim. ∎

Consider the topological space

∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v).\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v).

(g​f)w=g⁡(fg−1​w)∈cg​Γ​(w).(gf)_{w}=g(f_{g^{-1}w})\in c_{g\Gamma}(w).

By 2.39, the resulting family g​fgf is a well-defined element of ∏w∈Zg​Γcg​Γ​(w)\prod_{w\in Z_{g\Gamma}}c_{g\Gamma}(w). It is easy to see that this defines a group action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G).

Proposition 2.40.

There is an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant cubical isomorphism

(2.5) φ:RG→∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v).\varphi\colon R_{G}\to\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v).

Conversely, let

TφΓ​(N)=Sp⁡(Γ)∪⋃v∈DφΓ​(N){(v,φΓ​(N)v)}=Sp⁡(N)∪⋃v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(Sp⁡(N)){(v,pT​(v))}=T.T_{\varphi^{\Gamma}(N)}=\Sp(\Gamma)\cup\bigcup_{v\in D_{\varphi^{\Gamma}(N)}}\{(v,\varphi^{\Gamma}(N)_{v})\}=\Sp(N)\cup\bigcup_{v\in V(T)\setminus V(\Sp(N))}\{(v,p_{T}(v))\}=T.

rφΓ​(N)​(b)=φΓ​(N)b=r⁡(b).r_{\varphi^{\Gamma}(N)}(b)=\varphi^{\Gamma}(N)_{b}=r(b).

Now, let ff be a face of the product and v∈ZΓv\in Z_{\Gamma}. If v∈Bfv\in B_{f}, then

φΓ​(ψΓ​(f))v=rf​(v)=fv.\varphi^{\Gamma}(\psi^{\Gamma}(f))_{v}=r_{f}(v)=f_{v}.

We now verify that φΓ\varphi^{\Gamma} and ψΓ\psi^{\Gamma} are maps of posets. Consider a network realignment NN and a specification Nb→uN^{b\to u} of NN. The proof that the inverse map ψΓ\psi^{\Gamma} is order preserving is similar. Replacing an edge fvf_{v} with a vertex corresponds exactly to specifying vv.

We denote by

φ:RG→∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v).\varphi\colon R_{G}\to\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v).

the resulting isomorphism assembled from the isomorphisms φΓ\varphi_{\Gamma} on the individual connected components. It remains to show that φ\varphi is equivariant.

Let g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G) and let N=(T,r)∈ΓN=(T,r)\in\Gamma for some connected component Γ\Gamma of RGR_{G}. Then, for any w∈Zg​Γw\in Z_{g\Gamma}, if ww is unspecified in g​NgN, we have

φ​(g​N)w=(g​r)​(w)=g⁡(r⁡(g−1​w))=g⁡(φ​(N)g−1​w)=(g​φ​(N))w,\varphi(gN)_{w}=(gr)(w)=g(r(g^{-1}w))=g(\varphi(N)_{g^{-1}w})=(g\varphi(N))_{w},

Definition 2.41.

A vertex cc of a tree TT with nn vertices is called a centroid if all connected components of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} have at most n/2n/2 vertices.

A theorem of Jordan [14] states that every finite tree has either a unique centroid or exactly two adjacent centroids.

Lemma 2.42 ([14]).

Let TT be a tree on nn vertices. If nn is odd, TT has a unique centroid. If nn is even, then either TT has exactly one centroid, or two adjacent ones.

The main feature of centroids that interests us is that the set of centroids is preserved by every tree isomorphism. This allows us to construct a point in the geometric realisation of a tree that is fixed by any group action on the tree.

Definition 2.43.

The geometric center zgeom​(T)z_{\mathrm{geom}}(T) of a tree TT is defined to be the centroid of TT, viewed as a point in the geometric realisation of TT, if TT has a unique centroid, or the central point on the edge connecting the two centroids, if TT has two adjacent centroids.

Proposition 2.44.

The residual components RGR_{G} admit an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction onto a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-subspace DGD_{G}.

Proof.

It suffices to give an equivariant homotopy on

∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v)\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v)

between the identity and a map that collapses every connected component to a point. For a connected component Γ\Gamma, we choose this point to be (zgeom​(cΓ​(v)))v∈ZΓ(z_{\mathrm{geom}}(c_{\Gamma}(v)))_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}. Thus, under the identification from 2.40, the discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space is

DG={(zgeom​(cΓ​(v)))v∈ZΓ∣Γ∈π0​(RG)}.D_{G}=\{(z_{\mathrm{geom}}(c_{\Gamma}(v)))_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}\mid\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})\}.

Let TT be a tree and let zgeom​(T)z_{\mathrm{geom}}(T) be its geometric center. By HT:T×I→TH^{T}\colon T\times I\to T we denote the homotopy that linearly collapses TT to zgeom​(T)z_{\mathrm{geom}}(T). Since this homotopy is defined purely in terms of the metric on the geometric realisation of TT, and tree isomorphisms preserve the metric, this homotopy is also preserved by tree isomorphisms. This means that if f:T→T′f\colon T\to T^{\prime} is a tree isomorphism, then for any t∈It\in I and x∈Tx\in T, we have

(2.6) f⁡(HT​(x,t))=HT′​(f⁡(x),t).f(H^{T}(x,t))=H^{T^{\prime}}(f(x),t).

Now, for any connected component Γ\Gamma of RGR_{G}, we define

HΓ:(∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v))×I→∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v)H^{\Gamma}\colon\left(\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v)\right)\times I\to\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v)

via HΓ​(x,t)v=HcΓ​(v)​(xv,t)H^{\Gamma}(x,t)_{v}=H^{c_{\Gamma}(v)}(x_{v},t), whenever x∈∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v)x\in\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v) and t∈It\in I. The homotopies HΓH^{\Gamma} on ∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v)\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v) combine to give a homotopy

H:(∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v))×I→∐Γ∈π0​(RG)∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v).H\colon\left(\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v)\right)\times I\to\coprod_{\Gamma\in\pi_{0}(R_{G})}\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v).

The homotopy HH is Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant, because for any g∈Aut⁡(G)g\in\Aut(G) and x∈∏v∈ZΓcΓ​(v)x\in\prod_{v\in Z_{\Gamma}}c_{\Gamma}(v) we have

Hg​Γ​(g​x,t)w\displaystyle H^{g\Gamma}(gx,t)_{w} =Hcg​Γ​(w)​((g​x)w,t)\displaystyle=H^{c_{g\Gamma}(w)}\bigl((gx)_{w},t\bigr)
=Hcg​Γ​(w)​(g⁡(xg−1​w),t)\displaystyle=H^{c_{g\Gamma}(w)}\bigl(g(x_{g^{-1}w}),t\bigr)
=Hg​cΓ​(g−1​w)​(g⁡(xg−1​w),t)\displaystyle=H^{gc_{\Gamma}(g^{-1}w)}\bigl(g(x_{g^{-1}w}),t\bigr)
=(2.6)​g​(HcΓ​(g−1​w)​(xg−1​w,t))\displaystyle\overset{(\ref{isominv})}{=}g\left(H^{c_{\Gamma}(g^{-1}w)}(x_{g^{-1}w},t)\right)
=g⁡(HΓ​(x,t)g−1​w)\displaystyle=g\left(H^{\Gamma}(x,t)_{g^{-1}w}\right)
=(g​HΓ​(x,t))w.\displaystyle=\bigl(gH^{\Gamma}(x,t)\bigr)_{w}.

Hence, we have produced an equivariant strong deformation retraction onto a discrete Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-space. ∎

2.5. Examples

In this section we examine several examples of network realignment complexes for natural and relatively symmetric classes of base graphs. These examples already exhibit the phenomenon of having multiple connected components. Throughout, we apply the techniques and terminology developed in the previous sections, such as the spine and spine assignments of the connected components. We also investigate the action of the automorphism group of the base graph on the corresponding complex and determine the resulting orbit structure. For general base graphs, however, the enumeration of the connected components or even their orbits under the group action remains open, and the following examples will illustrate some of the challenges involved.

The first example is given by Kozlov [16], who showed that XKn≃KnX_{K_{n}}\simeq K_{n}. The present results strengthen this statement by taking the symmetry of the complex into account. The automorphism group of the base graph is given by Aut⁡(Kn)=Sn\Aut(K_{n})=S_{n}. Hence, we obtain the equivariant homotopy equivalence XKn≃SnKnX_{K_{n}}\simeq_{S_{n}}~K_{n}.

In the following examples, the base graph we consider is G=Kn∖E⁡(P)G=K_{n}\setminus E(P), where PP is a path of length kk and 0<k<n0<k<n. An automorphism of GG can either fix or reverse PP and can freely relabel the vertices not contained in PP. Hence, Aut⁡(G)≅Sn−k−1×C2\Aut(G)\cong S_{n-k-1}\times C_{2}, where C2C_{2} is the cyclic group with two elements.

Corollary 2.45.

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let G=Kn∖{e}G=K_{n}\setminus\{e\} for e∈E⁡(Kn)e\in E(K_{n}). Then XGX_{G} admits an (Sn−2×C2)(S_{n-2}\times C_{2})-equivariant strong deformation retraction onto Kn−2K_{n-2}.

Proof.

Let e=(u,w)e=(u,w). In the cubical complex XGX_{G}, the vertices uu and ww form a pair of mutual barriers. Since every network realignment contains at most one occupied leaf, no connected component other than the main component MGM_{G} can arise. The set of star trees is given by 𝒮G=[n]∖{u,w}\mathcal{S}_{G}=[n]\setminus\{u,w\}, and it follows from 2.33 that

XG≃(Sn−2×C2)K𝒮G≅Kn−2,X_{G}\simeq_{(S_{n-2}\times C_{2})}K_{\mathcal{S}_{G}}\cong K_{n-2},

which proves the claim. ∎

A projection of the above complex XGX_{G} for n=5n=5 is shown in Figure 2. Let e=(1,2)e=(1,2). The three grey 3-cubes connect the white star trees s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} and s3s_{3}. The violet squares attached to the star trees represent the cells with spine size one and a single occupied leaf. The following maximal cells do not have minimal spine: The blue 2-cubes correspond to cells with spine size two and no occupied leaf, and the red edges correspond to network realignments with spine size two and one occupied leaf. XGX_{G} admits a strong deformation retraction onto the main component MGM_{G}, which does not contain the blue and the red cells. The diagonals of the three grey 3-cubes connect the star trees and form the complete graph K3K_{3}, which is a strong deformation retract of XGX_{G}. The symmetric group S3S_{3} acts by permuting the star trees.

Corollary 2.46.

Assume n≥5n\geq 5. Let PP be a path of length two, and let G=Kn∖E⁡(P)G=K_{n}\setminus E(P). Then we have the following (Sn−3×C2)(S_{n-3}\times C_{2})-equivariant strong deformation retraction of XGX_{G}:

XG≃(Sn−3×C2)Kn−3∪∐i=1(n−3)​(n−4){∗},X_{G}\simeq_{(S_{n-3}\times C_{2})}K_{n-3}\cup\coprod\limits_{i=1}^{(n-3)(n-4)}\{\ast\},

where there are two orbits of connected components under the action of Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G).

Proof.

Since the argument is independent of the labelling, we denote P=(1,2,3)P=(1,2,3). After collapsing the complex Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariantly onto its minimal spine complex YGY_{G} by 2.21, it follows from 2.37 that every connected component distinct from MGM_{G} is uniquely determined by its spine and spine assignment.

We show that the Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-action on YGY_{G} has precisely two orbits of connected components, one of them containing only MGM_{G}. Let Γ\Gamma be any connected component of the other orbit. Its spine is of the form Sp⁡(Γ)=(x,2,y)\Sp(\Gamma)=(x,2,y) with x,y∈𝒮Gx,y\in\mathcal{S}_{G} being the occupied leaves. Indeed, a realignment can only contain two occupied leaves if the vertex 2 serves as a barrier for both 1 and 3. Without loss of generality, the spine assignment is given by cΓ​(1)={x},cΓ​(3)={y}c_{\Gamma}(1)=\{x\},c_{\Gamma}(3)=\{y\} and cΓ​(v)=Sp⁡(Γ)c_{\Gamma}(v)=\Sp(\Gamma) for every v∈[n]∖{1,2,3,x,y}v\in[n]\setminus\{1,2,3,x,y\}, since none of those vertices admits a barrier. As xx and yy may be chosen independently from 𝒮G={4,…,n}\mathcal{S}_{G}=\{4,\dots,n\}, which has cardinality (n−3)(n-3), the orbit contains (n−3)​(n−4)(n-3)(n-4) components. By 2.40, the residual components RGR_{G} admit an Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retract onto a discrete space. Furthermore, 2.33 yields MG≃Aut⁡(G)Kn−3M_{G}\simeq_{\Aut(G)}K_{n-3}, which finishes the proof. ∎

In the next example, the base graph is obtained from the complete graph by deleting a path of length three, where the different orbit types are depicted in Figure 7.

Corollary 2.47.

Assume n≥5n\geq 5. Let PP be a path of length three, and let G=Kn∖E⁡(P)G=K_{n}\setminus E(P). Then we have the following Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction of XGX_{G}:

XG≃(Sn−4×C2)Kn−4∪∐i=1f⁡(n){∗},X_{G}\simeq_{(S_{n-4}\times C_{2})}K_{n-4}\cup\coprod\limits_{i=1}^{f(n)}\{\ast\},

where

f⁡(n)=4​(n−4)​(n−5)​(∑k=0n−6(n−6k)​k!)+(n−4)​(n−3)+1,f(n)=4(n-4)(n-5)\left(\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-6}\binom{n-6}{k}k!\right)+(n-4)(n-3)+1,

and the union of points forms a discrete (Sn−4×C2)(S_{n-4}\times C_{2})-space containing (3​n−13)(3n-13) orbits.

Proof.

First assume n≥6.n\geq 6. For convenience, let P=(1,2,3,4)P=(1,2,3,4) denote the deleted path. As in the previous examples, by 2.21 we replace XGX_{G} with its Aut⁡(G)\Aut(G)-equivariantly retracted minimal spine complex YGY_{G} and analyse the connected components of YGY_{G}, whose network realignments contain at least two occupied leaves. By 2.37, each such component is uniquely determined by its spine and spine assignment. We analyse the possible spines and spine assignments in increasing order of spine size. The corresponding spines together with the vertices occupying the occupied leaves are illustrated in Figure 7.

There exists a single residual component with spine size one, namely Γ1\Gamma_{1}. The spine is given by Sp⁡(Γ1)=(1,4)\Sp(\Gamma_{1})=(1,4) and the vertices 1 and 4 are occupied by 3 and 2, respectively. For every vertex v∈𝒮Gv\in\mathcal{S}_{G}, one has cΓ1​(v)=Sp⁡(Γ1)c_{\Gamma_{1}}(v)=\Sp(\Gamma_{1}).

Next, we analyse the connected components of network realignments in YGY_{G} with spine size two, denoted by Γ2\Gamma^{2}. Let (u,γ2,w)(u,\gamma_{2},w) denote the spine of such a Γ∈Γ2\Gamma\in\Gamma^{2}. Since the spine is minimal, γ2\gamma_{2} is a barrier of the vertices γ1\gamma_{1} and γ3\gamma_{3}, which occupy uu and ww, respectively, for any realignment in Γ\Gamma. Hence, (γ1,γ2,γ3)(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}) is a subpath of PP. Without loss of generality, we may assume γ1∈{1,4}\gamma_{1}\in\{1,4\}. If γ1=1\gamma_{1}=1, then w∈[n]∖{γ1,γ2,γ3,4}w\in[n]\setminus\{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},4\} and u∈[n]∖{γ1,γ2,γ3,w}u\in[n]\setminus\{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},w\}. The same holds with 1 and 4 interchanged. Now, the spine assignments are uniquely determined. Therefore, we enumerate

|Γ2|=2​(n−4)2.|\Gamma^{2}|=2(n-4)^{2}.

All connected components with u∉{1,4}u\notin\{1,4\} belong to the same orbit, denoted Γ12\Gamma^{2}_{1}. Further, all connected components with u∈{1,4}u\in\{1,4\} belong to a second orbit, denoted by Γ22\Gamma^{2}_{2}, since the C2C_{2}-action interchanges the subpaths (1,2,3)(1,2,3) and (2,3,4)(2,3,4) as well as 11 and 44.

Finally, we analyse the connected components of network realignments in YGY_{G} with spine size greater than two. Note that no vertex is a barrier of more than two vertices. Hence, the only possibility for the spine to have all leaves occupied is to be path-shaped. We distinguish two classes of network realignments: those in which both vertices 2 and 3 lie in the spine, and those in which they do not.

Similarly, we divide the second class into families of connected components according to spine size i+2i+2, denoted (Γi4)(\Gamma_{i}^{4}). 1+2+2​(n−5)+(n−6)=3​n−13.1+2+2(n-5)+(n-6)=3n-13.

The topology of the main component is given by 2.33.
