The preceding case already illustrates the rapid growth of (orbits of) connected components as the number of omitted edges increases, as well as the difficulty of enumerating them. While the components in the present example are still characterised by path-shaped spines, this feature is no longer preserved once more than three edges are removed or when three deleted edges do not themselves form a path. The authors leave this as an open problem.

3. Geometry of the Network Realignment Graph 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}

In the previous section we studied the equivariant topology of the network realignment complex XGX_{G} over an arbitrary connected base graph GG. We now specialise to the complete base graph KnK_{n} and turn from topology to geometry. More precisely, instead of studying the homotopy type of the cubical complex XnX_{n}, we study the graph metric on its 11-skeleton. This graph records the possible single leaf slides between labelled spanning trees, and its metric measures the minimal number of such slides needed to pass from one tree to another.

Definition 3.1.

The network realignment graph 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is the 11-skeleton of the network realignment complex Xn=XKnX_{n}=X_{K_{n}}, where KnK_{n} has vertex set [n][n]. Equivalently, the vertices of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} are the spanning trees of KnK_{n}, or labelled trees on [n][n], and two vertices are adjacent if the corresponding trees differ by a single leaf slide.

The study of the geometry of the network realignment graph is motivated by Kozlov’s work on network realignment complexes. Kozlov asks in [16] whether one can give a formula for the diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. We recall the relevant notions.

Definition 3.2.

We write d𝒢nd_{\mathcal{G}_{n}} for the graph distance on 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. Thus d𝒢n​(T1,T2)d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},T_{2}) is the smallest number of leaf slides needed to transform T1T_{1} into T2T_{2}. The diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is given by

diam⁡(𝒢n)=maxT1,T2∈V⁡(𝒢n)⁡d𝒢n​(T1,T2).\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{G}_{n})=\max_{T_{1},T_{2}\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n})}d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},T_{2}).

The main result of this section is a pair of explicit upper and lower bounds. They are summarised in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.3.

Let n≥3n\geq 3. The diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} satisfies

⌊3​n2−4​n8⌋≤diam⁡(𝒢n)≤n22−n,\left\lfloor\frac{3n^{2}-4n}{8}\right\rfloor\leq\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{G}_{n})\leq\frac{n^{2}}{2}-n,

if nn is even and

⌊3​n2−6​n8⌋≤diam⁡(𝒢n)≤n2−12−n,\left\lfloor\frac{3n^{2}-6n}{8}\right\rfloor\leq\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{G}_{n})\leq\frac{n^{2}-1}{2}-n,

if nn is odd.

The proof of the upper bound occupies the next three subsections. We first introduce two quantities, Φc\Phi_{c} and Ψ\Psi, which respectively give an upper and a lower estimate for the distance from a tree to a star tree. We then characterise the vertices for which these estimates agree in terms of centroids. The upper bound for the diameter is then obtained by choosing, for any pair of trees, a distance-minimising star tree for each of the two given trees and constructing a path that passes through both star trees.

The lower bound is proved in the last subsection. We introduce the matching distance, an auxiliary metric on 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}, which bounds the graph distance from below, and determine the exact diameter of the network realignment graph with respect to this distance. This gives us the desired lower bound.

Computations suggest that the upper bound is sharp for all n≥6n\geq 6. We have verified that it agrees with the exact diameter for all 6≤n≤96\leq n\leq 9. However, exact computations quickly become infeasible, because by Cayley’s formula, 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} has nn−2n^{n-2} vertices, and hence its size grows superexponentially in nn.

Beyond the diameter bounds, the methods developed in this section also reveal additional structure in the geometry of the realignment graph. In particular, the characterisation of nearest star trees is an interesting structural consequences of the theory developed in this section. Some aspects of this metric rigidity will also play a role in the next section, where we determine the automorphism group of XnX_{n}.

3.1. Distances to Star Trees

The invariant Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) depends on a chosen vertex cc and measures how far TT is from the star tree scs_{c} by summing the excess distances from cc. The invariant Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T) measures, edge by edge, how balanced the cuts of TT are.

The main point of this subsection is that Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T) gives a lower bound for the distance from TT to any star tree, while Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) gives an upper bound for the distance from TT to the specific star tree scs_{c}. In the next subsection, we determine exactly when these two bounds agree (cf. 3.14).

Definition 3.4.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a tree. Let c∈[n]c\in[n] be any vertex of TT. We define

Φc​(T)=∑x∈V⁡(T)∖{c}(dT​(x,c)−1).\Phi_{c}(T)=\sum_{x\in V(T)\setminus\{c\}}(d_{T}(x,c)-1).

For every very edge ee of TT, removing ee from TT leaves us with a forest consisting of exactly two trees AeA_{e} and BeB_{e}. We define

σT​(e)=min⁡(|V⁡(Ae)|,|V⁡(Be)|)\sigma_{T}(e)=\min(|V(A_{e})|,|V(B_{e})|)

and

Ψ⁡(T)=∑e∈E⁡(T)(σT​(e)−1).\Psi(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}(\sigma_{T}(e)-1).
Lemma 3.5.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a spanning tree. Let c∈[n]c\in[n] be any vertex of TT. Then TT is a star tree if and only if Ψ⁡(T)=0\Psi(T)=0. Further, TT is a star tree centered at cc if and only if Φc​(T)=0\Phi_{c}(T)=0.

Proof.

This follows immediately from the definitions. ∎

Lemma 3.6.

Let N=(T,r)N=(T,r) be a 1-dimensional realignment (i.e. leaf slide). We write B={v}B=\{v\} and r⁡(v)=(u,w)r(v)=(u,w). Let c∈V⁡(T)=[n]∖{v}c\in V(T)=[n]\setminus\{v\}.

In this situation, the leaf slide changes the values of Ψ\Psi by at most one. To be precise, we have

(3.1) |Ψ⁡(Nv→u)−Ψ⁡(Nv→w)|=1​, if n is even, and|Ψ⁡(Nv→u)−Ψ⁡(Nv→w)|≤1​, if n is odd.\begin{split}|\Psi(N^{v\to u})-\Psi(N^{v\to w})|&=1\text{, if $n$ is even, and}\\ |\Psi(N^{v\to u})-\Psi(N^{v\to w})|&\leq 1\text{, if $n$ is odd.}\end{split}

The behaviour of Φ\Phi depends on whether the slide is performed towards or away from cc. Let γ\gamma be the unique path connecting ww and cc in TT, then

(3.2) Φc​(Nv→u)={Φc​(Nv→w)−1,if u lies on γ,Φc​(Nv→w)+1,otherwise.\Phi_{c}(N^{v\to u})=\begin{cases}\Phi_{c}(N^{v\to w})-1,&\text{if $u$ lies on $\gamma$,}\\ \Phi_{c}(N^{v\to w})+1,&\text{otherwise.}\\ \end{cases}
Remark 3.7.

It is important to note that, if the leaf vv that is being slid is equal to cc, then Φc\Phi_{c} may change by more than one under a leaf slide.

Proof of 3.6.

We first show (3.1). Given any edge ee of any tree TT, we want to compare the connected components AeA_{e} and BeB_{e} that are obtained by removing ee from TT, for different choices of TT. To keep the notation consistent while considering different trees, we fix an arbitrary orientation on the edges of KnK_{n}. Now, we can redefine AeTA_{e}^{T} to be the connected component of T∖{e}T\setminus\{e\}, that contains the source of ee and BeTB_{e}^{T} to be the connected component that contains the sink of ee.

To simplify notation, we write Tu=Tv→uT_{u}=T^{v\to u} and Tw=Tv→wT_{w}=T^{v\to w}. Consider the edges (v,u)(v,u) in TuT_{u} and (v,w)(v,w) in TwT_{w}. Since both of these edges are leaf edges, they do not contribute to Ψ⁡(Tu)\Psi(T_{u}) and Ψ⁡(Tw)\Psi(T_{w}), respectively.

The other edges of Ψ⁡(Tu)\Psi(T_{u}) are precisely those which the two trees have in common. Let ee be any of these shared edges other than (u,w)(u,w). Then the leaf slide clearly preserves the vertices in AeA_{e} and BeB_{e}. Hence, we see that σTu​(e)=σTw​(e)\sigma_{T_{u}}(e)=\sigma_{T_{w}}(e). This shows that

|Ψ⁡(Tu)−Ψ⁡(Tw)|=|∑e∈E⁡(Tu)σTu​(e)−∑e∈E⁡(Tw)σTw​(e)|=|σTu​(u,w)−σTw​(u,w)|.\begin{split}|\Psi(T_{u})-\Psi(T_{w})|&=\left|\sum_{e\in E(T_{u})}\sigma_{T_{u}}(e)-\sum_{e\in E(T_{w})}\sigma_{T_{w}}(e)\right|\\ &=|\sigma_{T_{u}}(u,w)-\sigma_{T_{w}}(u,w)|.\end{split}

Without loss of generality, we may assume that the edge e=(u,w)e=(u,w) is oriented from uu to ww. Hence, we have V⁡(AeTw)=V⁡(AeTu)∖{v}V(A_{e}^{T_{w}})=V(A_{e}^{T_{u}})\setminus\{v\} and V⁡(BeTw)=V⁡(BeTu)∪{v}V(B_{e}^{T_{w}})=V(B_{e}^{T_{u}})\cup\{v\}. It follows that

|σTu​(u,w)−σTw​(u,w)|=|min⁡(|V⁡(AeTu)|,|V⁡(BeTu)|)−min⁡(|V⁡(AeTw)|,|V⁡(BeTw)|)|=|min⁡(|V⁡(AeTu)|,|V⁡(BeTu)|)−min⁡(|V⁡(AeTu)|−1,|V⁡(BeTu)|+1)|≤1\begin{multlined}|\sigma_{T_{u}}(u,w)-\sigma_{T_{w}}(u,w)|=\left|\min(|V(A_{e}^{T_{u}})|,|V(B_{e}^{T_{u}})|)-\min(|V(A_{e}^{T_{w}})|,|V(B_{e}^{T_{w}})|)\right|\\ =\left|\min(|V(A_{e}^{T_{u}})|,|V(B_{e}^{T_{u}})|)-\min(|V(A_{e}^{T_{u}})|-1,|V(B_{e}^{T_{u}})|+1)\right|\leq 1\end{multlined}

Let a=|V⁡(AeTu)|a=|V(A_{e}^{T_{u}})|, then |V⁡(BeTu)|=n−a|V(B_{e}^{T_{u}})|=n-a. Notice that since nn is even, both of aa and n−an-a have the same parity and both of a−1a-1 and n−a+1n-a+1 have the opposite parity to that of aa. This means that

|Ψ⁡(Tu)−Ψ⁡(Tw)|=|min⁡(a,n−a)−min⁡(a−1,n−a+1)||\Psi(T_{u})-\Psi(T_{w})|=|\min(a,n-a)-\min(a-1,n-a+1)|

must be odd, which is only possible if it is equal to one. This concludes the proof of (3.1).

To prove (3.2), it suffices to consider the case where uu lies on γ\gamma. The other case follows by reversing the roles of uu and ww. Hence, our goal is to show that

Φc​(Tw)−Φc​(Tu)=1\Phi_{c}(T_{w})-\Phi_{c}(T_{u})=1

under the assumption that uu lies on γ\gamma.

Let xx be any vertex other than vv. Since vv is a leaf in both TuT_{u} and TwT_{w}, the unique path connecting xx to cc in either of the two trees does not contain vv. Since Tw∖{v}=Tu∖{v}T_{w}\setminus\{v\}=T_{u}\setminus\{v\}, this means that the two paths are identical, so dTu​(x,c)=dTw​(x,c)d_{T_{u}}(x,c)=d_{T_{w}}(x,c). This shows that

Φc​(Tw)−Φc​(Tu)=∑x∈V⁡(Tw)dTw​(x,c)−∑x∈V⁡(Tu)dTu​(x,c)=dTw​(v,c)−dTu​(v,c).\begin{split}\Phi_{c}(T_{w})-\Phi_{c}(T_{u})&=\sum_{x\in V(T_{w})}d_{T_{w}}(x,c)-\sum_{x\in V(T_{u})}d_{T_{u}}(x,c)\\ &=d_{T_{w}}(v,c)-d_{T_{u}}(v,c).\end{split}

Since uu lies on γ\gamma and ww is connected to uu, we know that in both trees d⁡(w,c)=d⁡(u,c)+1d(w,c)=d(u,c)+1. dTw​(v,c)−dTu​(v,c)=dTw​(w,c)+1−(dTu​(u,c)+1)=dTu​(u,c)+1−dTu​(u,c)=1,\begin{split}d_{T_{w}}(v,c)-d_{T_{u}}(v,c)&=d_{T_{w}}(w,c)+1-(d_{T_{u}}(u,c)+1)\\ &=d_{T_{u}}(u,c)+1-d_{T_{u}}(u,c)\\ &=1,\end{split}

which concludes the proof of (3.2). ∎

Proposition 3.8.

Let n≥2n\geq 2. 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is bipartite if and only if nn is even.

Proof.

Let nn be even. Consider the map

V⁡(𝒢n)→{±1},T↦(−1)Ψ⁡(T).V(\mathcal{G}_{n})\to\{\pm 1\},\quad T\mapsto(-1)^{\Psi(T)}.

It is an immediate consequence of 3.6 that this is a 2-coloring on 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}.

Now, let n≥3n\geq 3 be odd. We will construct a cycle of odd length to show that 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is not bipartite.

For any two distinct a,b∈[n]a,b\in[n], let γa,b\gamma_{a,b} be a path between sas_{a} and sbs_{b} in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} consisting of the n−2n-2 leaf slides for each of which a vertex x∈[n]∖{a,b}x\in[n]\setminus\{a,b\} is slid along the edge (a,b)(a,b), in an arbitrary order.

For three pairwise distinct points a,b,ca,b,c, the concatenation γa,b∗γb,c∗γc,a\gamma_{a,b}*\gamma_{b,c}*\gamma_{c,a} is a cycle of length 3​(n−2)3(n-2), which is odd. ∎

Lemma 3.9.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a spanning tree. Let c∈V⁡(T)c\in V(T) be any vertex of TT. Then

Ψ⁡(T)≤d𝒢n​(T,sc)≤Φc​(T).\Psi(T)\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})\leq\Phi_{c}(T).
Proof.

We first show the inequality Ψ⁡(T)≤d𝒢n​(T,sc)\Psi(T)\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c}). Let k=d𝒢n​(T,sc)k=d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c}). Then there exists a sequence of T=T0,T1,…,Tk=scT=T_{0},T_{1},\dots,T_{k}=s_{c}, such that each two consecutive trees are related via a single leaf slide.

Applying Ψ\Psi to this sequence gives a sequence of integers Ψ⁡(T0),…,Ψ⁡(Tk)\Psi(T_{0}),\dots,\Psi(T_{k}), which starts at Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T) and ends at Ψ⁡(sc)=0\Psi(s_{c})=0. Since any two consecutive trees are related by a leaf slide, it follows from 3.6 that this sequence changes by at most one each step. Hence, the sequence must have length k≥Ψ⁡(T)k\geq\Psi(T).

Now, suppose that UU is any spanning tree on nn vertices. We define a new spanning tree f⁡(U)f(U) as follows. If U=scU=s_{c}, then f⁡(U)=Uf(U)=U. For any tree UU other than scs_{c}, pick an arbitrary leaf vv, which has distance at least 22 from cc. Let (v,w,u,…,c)(v,w,u,\dots,c) be the unique path between vv and cc in UU. We now define f⁡(U)f(U) to be the tree obtained by sliding the leaf vv along the edge (w,u)(w,u).

Notice that in the case where U≠scU\neq s_{c}, the vertex ww is not equal to cc, because dU​(v,c)≥2d_{U}(v,c)\geq 2. Hence, uu lies on the unique path connecting ww and cc in UU, so it follows from 3.6 that Φc​(f⁡(U))=Φc​(U)−1\Phi_{c}(f(U))=\Phi_{c}(U)-1.

Applying ff repeatedly to our tree TT yields a sequence T=T0,…,Tl=scT=T_{0},\dots,T_{l}=s_{c} starting at TT and ending at scs_{c}, such that Ti+1=f⁡(Ti)T_{i+1}=f(T_{i}) for each ii. In particular, consecutive trees in this sequence are related via a leaf slide, so the sequence describes a path in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. This path must have length Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T), because Φc\Phi_{c} decreases by exactly one at each step and Φc​(sc)=0\Phi_{c}(s_{c})=0. We conclude that d𝒢n​(T,sc)≤Φc​(T)d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})\leq\Phi_{c}(T).

∎

Remark 3.10.

Notice that this argument does not show that d𝒢n​(T,sc)=Φc​(T)d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})=\Phi_{c}(T), because a leaf slide of cc may decrease Φc\Phi_{c} by more than one.

In fact, equality in the above equation does not hold in general. A counterexample is obtained by considering a path tree TT, and choosing cc to be one of its two leaves. For large nn, it is more efficient to first slide the leaf to the middle of the path tree and then slide the rest of the tree towards cc, instead of sliding the entire tree towards cc immediately.

3.2. Centroids and Nearest Star Trees

The above counterexample depends on T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} having a large component. Sliding cc toward this component decreases the distance to each of its vertices by one while increasing the distance to every other vertex by one. If the component contains more than half of the vertices, Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) decreases by more than one. Conversely, if no such component exists, then every leaf slide of cc increases Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T). This observation yields a criterion for equality in the preceding inequality.

Definition 3.11.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a spanning tree and let c∈[n]c\in[n]. Removing cc from TT leaves a forest. We define

Fc​(T)=max⁡{|V⁡(C)|∣C​ is a connected component of ​T∖{c}}.F_{c}(T)=\max\{|V(C)|\mid C\text{ is a connected component of }T\setminus\{c\}\}.

Recall from 2.41, that cc is a centroid of TT if and only if

Fc​(T)≤n2.F_{c}(T)\leq\frac{n}{2}.
Lemma 3.12.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a spanning tree and let c∈V⁡(T)c\in V(T). For each edge e∈E⁡(T)e\in E(T), let AecA_{e}^{c} be the connected component of T∖{e}T\setminus\{e\} which does not contain cc, and write aec=|V⁡(Aec)|a_{e}^{c}=|V(A_{e}^{c})|. Then

Φc​(T)−Ψ⁡(T)=∑e∈E⁡(T)max⁡(0,2​aec−n).\Phi_{c}(T)-\Psi(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}\max(0,2a_{e}^{c}-n).

In particular, Φc​(T)=Ψ​(T)\Phi_{c}(T)=\Psi(T) if and only if cc is a centroid of TT.

Proof.

We first show that

Φc​(T)=∑e∈E⁡(T)(aec−1).\Phi_{c}(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}(a_{e}^{c}-1).

Since TT has n−1n-1 edges, this equality is equivalent to

∑e∈E⁡(T)aec​(T)=∑x∈V⁡(T)dT​(x,c).\sum_{e\in E(T)}a_{e}^{c}(T)=\sum_{x\in V(T)}d_{T}(x,c).

Now, consider any vertex x≠cx\neq c. For any given e∈E⁡(T)e\in E(T), xx lies in AecA_{e}^{c} if and only if ee lies on the unique path connecting xx and cc. Hence, the vertex xx contributes one to the left hand side for each edge on the unique path between xx and cc. This path contains exactly dT​(x,c)d_{T}(x,c) edges, so the equality follows.

The two connected components of T∖{e}T\setminus\{e\} have sizes aeca_{e}^{c} and n−aecn-a_{e}^{c}, so σT​(e)=min⁡(aec,n−aec)\sigma_{T}(e)=\min(a_{e}^{c},n-a_{e}^{c}). Thus

Φc​(T)−Ψ⁡(T)=∑e∈E⁡(T)(aec​(T)−min⁡(aec,n−aec))=∑e∈E⁡(T)max⁡(0,2​aec−n).\Phi_{c}(T)-\Psi(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}\left(a_{e}^{c}(T)-\min(a_{e}^{c},n-a_{e}^{c})\right)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}\max(0,2a_{e}^{c}-n).

It remains to characterise when the right hand side vanishes. The connected components of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} are exactly the subtrees AecA_{e}^{c} for those edges ee incident to cc. Every other subtree AecA_{e}^{c} is contained in one of these components. Hence

Fc​(T)=maxe∈E⁡(T)⁡aec.F_{c}(T)=\max_{e\in E(T)}a_{e}^{c}.

Therefore, Φc​(T)=Ψ​(T)\Phi_{c}(T)=\Psi(T) if and only if aec≤n/2a_{e}^{c}\leq n/2 for every edge ee. This is equivalent to Fc​(T)≤n/2F_{c}(T)\leq n/2, that is, cc is a centroid. ∎

Lemma 3.13.

Let c∈[n]c\in[n]. If T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} are related by a leaf slide and Fc​(T1)>n2F_{c}(T_{1})>\frac{n}{2} but Fc​(T2)<Fc​(T1)F_{c}(T_{2})<F_{c}(T_{1}), then

Let T2T_{2} be obtained from T1T_{1} by sliding the leaf edge (v,u)∈E⁡(T1)(v,u)\in E(T_{1}) along the edge e=(u,w)e=(u,w). Since Fc​(T1)>n/2F_{c}(T_{1})>n/2, there is a unique component CC of T1∖{c}T_{1}\setminus\{c\} with |V⁡(C)|>n/2|V(C)|>n/2.

The only way for the leaf slide to decrease FcF_{c} is for the leaf vv to be reattached from the component CC directly to cc. Hence, w=cw=c and u∈V⁡(C)u\in V(C).

As in the proof of 3.6, the only edge whose contribution to Ψ\Psi changes is e=(u,c)e=(u,c). Set q=|V⁡(C)|q=|V(C)|. Then

σT1​(e)=n−q.\sigma_{T_{1}}(e)=n-q.

After the slide, the two components of T2∖{e}T_{2}\setminus\{e\} have sizes q−1q-1 and n−q+1n-q+1. Therefore,

σT2​(e)=min⁡(q−1,n−q+1)≥n−q=σT1​(e).\sigma_{T_{2}}(e)=\min(q-1,n-q+1)\geq n-q=\sigma_{T_{1}}(e).

Hence, Ψ⁡(T2)≥Ψ⁡(T1)\Psi(T_{2})\geq\Psi(T_{1}). ∎

Proposition 3.14.

Let T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) be a spanning tree and let c∈V⁡(T)c\in V(T). Then the following are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    cc is a centroid of TT.

  2. (2)

    Ψ⁡(T)=d𝒢n​(T,sc)=Φc​(T)\Psi(T)=d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})=\Phi_{c}(T).

  3. (3)

    scs_{c} has minimal distance from TT in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} among all star trees.

Proof.

The equivalence of (2)(\ref{equalities}) and (1)(\ref{central}) follows immediately from 3.12 and 3.9.

Suppose (2)(\ref{equalities}) holds. By 3.9, Ψ⁡(T)≤d𝒢n​(T,sa)\Psi(T)\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{a}) for each star tree sas_{a}. On the other hand, (2)(\ref{equalities}) states that d𝒢n​(T,sc)=Ψ⁡(T)d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})=\Psi(T). Thus, scs_{c} has minimal distance from TT among all star trees. This proves (2)⇒(3)(\ref{equalities})\Rightarrow(\ref{minstar}).

It remains to prove (3)⇒(1)(\ref{minstar})\Rightarrow(\ref{central}). Choose a centroid dd of TT, which exists by 2.42. By the already proved implication (1)⇒(2)(\ref{central})\Rightarrow(\ref{equalities}), we have d𝒢n​(T,sd)=Ψ⁡(T)d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{d})=\Psi(T). 3.9 gives Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T) as a lower bound for the distance from TT to any star tree. Hence, every distance-minimising star tree has distance exactly Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T) from TT.

Now, assume that scs_{c} is distance-minimising, and suppose that cc is not a centroid of TT. Then

Fc​(T)>n2.F_{c}(T)>\frac{n}{2}.

Let T=T0,T1,…,Tk=scT=T_{0},T_{1},\dots,T_{k}=s_{c} be a shortest path from TT to scs_{c} in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. Since scs_{c} is distance-minimising, we have k=d𝒢n​(T,sc)=Ψ⁡(T)k=d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T,s_{c})=\Psi(T).

By 3.6, the value of Ψ\Psi changes by at most one under each leaf slide. Since Ψ⁡(T0)=Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T_{0})=\Psi(T) and Ψ⁡(Tk)=Ψ⁡(sc)=0\Psi(T_{k})=\Psi(s_{c})=0, and since the path has length Ψ⁡(T)\Psi(T), the value of Ψ\Psi must decrease by exactly one at each step.

Conversely, Fc​(T0)>n2F_{c}(T_{0})>\frac{n}{2} and Fc​(Tk)=Fc​(sc)=1≤n2F_{c}(T_{k})=F_{c}(s_{c})=1\leq\frac{n}{2}. Hence, there exists an index ii such that Fc​(Ti)>n2F_{c}(T_{i})>\frac{n}{2} and Fc​(Ti+1)<Fc​(Ti)F_{c}(T_{i+1})<F_{c}(T_{i}). By 3.13, this implies that

Ψ⁡(Ti+1)≥Ψ⁡(Ti),\Psi(T_{i+1})\geq\Psi(T_{i}),

contradicting the fact that Ψ\Psi decreases by exactly one at each step. Therefore, cc is a centroid of TT. ∎

3.3. An Upper Bound for the Diameter

The previous analysis showed that it suffices to study the quantity Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) for centroids cc of TT to determine the distance to the closest star tree. To bound Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) from above, we introduce two optimisation problems: the first one analyses the structure of the connected components of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\}, and the second one enumerates their number. This upper bound allows us to bound the distance between any two network realignments by passing through their respective closest star trees.

Lemma 3.15.

For any vertex cc of TT, we have

Φc​(T)≤(n−2)​(n−1)2.\Phi_{c}(T)\leq\frac{(n-2)(n-1)}{2}.

Equality holds if and only if TT is a path tree and cc is a leaf of TT.

Proof.

For a fixed n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, consider the following optimisation problem.

maxα1,α2,…\displaystyle\max_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots} ∑i≥1(i−1)​αi\displaystyle\sum_{i\geq 1}(i-1)\alpha_{i}
subject to: αi∈ℤ≥0\displaystyle\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} ∀i≥1\displaystyle\forall i\geq 1
∑i≥1αi=(n−1)\displaystyle\sum_{i\geq 1}\alpha_{i}=(n-1)
αi=0⇒αi+1=0\displaystyle\alpha_{i}=0\Rightarrow\alpha_{i+1}=0 ∀i≥1\displaystyle\forall i\geq 1

Solutions (αi)i≥1(\alpha_{i})_{i\geq 1} to this optimisation problem can be interpreted as the number of vertices of distance ii from the root cc in a rooted tree TT with nn vertices. In this situation, we get

Φc​(T)=∑i≥1(i−1)​αi.\Phi_{c}(T)=\sum_{i\geq 1}(i-1)\alpha_{i}.

Suppose that (αi)i≥1(\alpha_{i})_{i\geq 1} is a solution to this problem with αk>1\alpha_{k}>1 for some kk. The constraints of the problem force there to be a j≥1j\geq 1 for which αj≠0\alpha_{j}\neq 0 and αi=0\alpha_{i}=0 for all i>ji>j. From the given solution we obtain a new solution by replacing αk\alpha_{k} with 11 and αj+1\alpha_{j+1} with αk−1\alpha_{k}-1. This is a strictly better solution.

Hence, any optimal solution is one which contains only ones and zeroes. But the only such solution is α1=⋯=αn−1=1\alpha_{1}=\dots=\alpha_{n-1}=1 and αi=0\alpha_{i}=0 for i≥ni\geq n. This corresponds to path trees rooted at one of their leaves.

The value attained by this unique optimal solution is

∑i=1n−1(i−1)=(n−2)​(n−1)2.\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(i-1)=\frac{(n-2)(n-1)}{2}.

This proves the assertion. ∎

Lemma 3.16.

Let cc be a centroid of TT. Then

Φc​(T)≤⌊n24⌋−n+1.\Phi_{c}(T)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor-n+1.

Equality holds if and only if TT is a path tree.

Proof.

The assertion is immediate for n=2n=2, so assume n≥3n\geq 3. We first rewrite Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) in terms of the connected components of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\}. Let v1,…,vkv_{1},\ldots,v_{k} be the neighbours of cc, and let ViV_{i} denote the connected component of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} that contains viv_{i}. For any vertex x∈Vix\in V_{i}, the unique path from xx to cc in TT must contain viv_{i}. Thus, dT​(x,c)=dVi​(x,vi)+1d_{T}(x,c)=d_{V_{i}}(x,v_{i})+1. It follows that

Φc​(T)\displaystyle\Phi_{c}(T) =∑x∈V⁡(T)∖{c}(dT​(x,c)−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in V(T)\setminus\{c\}}(d_{T}(x,c)-1)
=∑i=1k∑x∈VidVi​(x,vi)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{x\in V_{i}}d_{V_{i}}(x,v_{i})
=n−k−1+∑i=1k∑x∈Vi∖{vi}(dVi​(x,vi)−1)\displaystyle=n-k-1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{x\in V_{i}\setminus\{v_{i}\}}(d_{V_{i}}(x,v_{i})-1)
=n−k−1+∑i=1kΦvi​(Vi).\displaystyle=n-k-1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Phi_{v_{i}}(V_{i}).

By 3.15, we get

Φvi​(Vi)≤(di−1)​(di−2)2,\Phi_{v_{i}}(V_{i})\leq\frac{(d_{i}-1)(d_{i}-2)}{2},

where did_{i} is the number of vertices of ViV_{i}.

Now, we consider another optimisation problem to analyse the number and structure of the connected components that maximise Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T). For d=(di)i≥1d=(d_{i})_{i\geq 1}, we define

K⁡(d)=∑i≥1di​(di−1)2=∑i≥1((di−1)​(di−2)2+di−1).K(d)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\frac{d_{i}(d_{i}-1)}{2}=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left(\frac{(d_{i}-1)(d_{i}-2)}{2}+d_{i}-1\right).

The shift ensures that indices with di=0d_{i}=0 do not contribute to K⁡(d)K(d), allowing to sum over all i≥1i\geq 1. For a fixed n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, consider the following optimisation problem.

maxd=(d1,d2,…)\displaystyle\max_{d=(d_{1},d_{2},\dots)} K⁡(d)\displaystyle K(d)
subject to: di∈ℤ≥0\displaystyle d_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} ∀i≥1\displaystyle\forall i\geq 1
di≤n2\displaystyle d_{i}\leq\frac{n}{2} ∀i≥1\displaystyle\forall i\geq 1
di≤di−1\displaystyle d_{i}\leq d_{i-1} ∀i≥2\displaystyle\forall i\geq 2
∑i≥1di=(n−1)\displaystyle\sum_{i\geq 1}d_{i}=(n-1)

Note that the non-zero did_{i}’s of a solution can be interpreted as the sizes of the connected components ViV_{i} of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} of a rooted tree (T,c)(T,c), ordered decreasingly. In this situation, we get

K⁡(d)≥Φc​(T)K(d)\geq\Phi_{c}(T)

using 3.15. Equality holds if and only if all ViV_{i}’s are path trees. Consequently, to maximise Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T), each connected component of T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} must be a path tree.

We claim that the unique optimal solution to this problem is given by d1=⌊n/2⌋d_{1}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor, d2=(n−1)−d1d_{2}=(n-1)-d_{1}, and di=0d_{i}=0 for i≥3i\geq 3. This corresponds to trees for which T∖{c}T\setminus\{c\} has only two connected components. Consequently, the value of Φc​(T)\Phi_{c}(T) is maximal if and only if TT is a path tree. The value of the unique optimal solution is

K⁡(d)=12​⌊n2⌋​(⌊n2⌋−1)+12​(n−⌊n2⌋−1)​(n−⌊n2⌋−2)=⌊n24⌋−n+1.K(d)=\frac{1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-1\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(n-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-1\right)\left(n-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-2\right)=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor-n+1.

Let dd be a solution that is not of the claimed form. Then there exist indices i<ji<j with di<⌊n/2⌋d_{i}<\lfloor n/2\rfloor and dj>0d_{j}>0. Choose such i,ji,j with i<ji<j, and move one unit from djd_{j} to did_{i}. After reordering, the resulting sequence again satisfies the constraints, and the value of KK increases by di−dj+1≥1d_{i}-d_{j}+1\geq 1. Hence, dd is not optimal. ∎

Lemma 3.17.

Let a,b∈[n]a,b\in[n] be two distinct numbers. Then d𝒢n​(sa,sb)=n−2d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(s_{a},s_{b})=n-2.

Proof.

A quick calculation shows that Φa​(sb)=n−2\Phi_{a}(s_{b})=n-2. Thus by 3.9 we have d𝒢n​(sa,sb)≤n−2d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(s_{a},s_{b})\leq n-2.

Conversely, since every x∈[n]∖{a,b}x\in[n]\setminus\{a,b\} defines a leaf edge (x,a)(x,a) in sas_{a} and none of these edges exist in sbs_{b}, any sequence of leaf slides connecting the two star trees must slide the edge (x,a)(x,a) at least once. Hence, d𝒢n​(sa,sb)≥n−2d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(s_{a},s_{b})\geq n-2. ∎

Theorem 3.18.

For any n≥2n\geq 2 the diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is bounded from above by ⌊n22⌋−n\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{2}\right\rfloor-n.

Proof.

Let T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} be arbitrary spanning trees. By 2.42 there exists a centroid c1∈V⁡(T1)c_{1}\in V(T_{1}) (respectively c2∈V⁡(T2)c_{2}\in V(T_{2})). Using Lemmas 3.9, 3.16, 3.17 and the triangle inequality, we find that

d𝒢n​(T1,T2)≤d𝒢n​(T1,sc1)+d𝒢n​(sc1,sc2)+d𝒢n​(sc2,T2)≤Φc1​(T1)+(n−2)+Φc2​(T2)≤2​(⌊n24⌋−n+1)+n−2=⌊n22⌋−n.\begin{split}d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},T_{2})&\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},s_{c_{1}})+d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(s_{c_{1}},s_{c_{2}})+d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(s_{c_{2}},T_{2})\\ &\leq\Phi_{c_{1}}(T_{1})+(n-2)+\Phi_{c_{2}}(T_{2})\\ &\leq 2\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor-n+1\right)+n-2\\ &=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{2}\right\rfloor-n.\end{split}

This concludes the proof. ∎

3.4. Matching Distance and Lower Bounds

For the lower bound, we introduce an auxiliary metric that bounds the graph distance from below. Unlike the graph distance, this metric does not depend on the structure of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}. Instead, it solely compares distances between certain vertices within the considered trees. In this metric, the distance between certain network realignments can be calculated explicitly, yielding a lower bound.

Definition 3.19.

A matching ℳ\mathcal{M} on [n][n] is a set of disjoint 2-element subsets of [n][n]. Given a matching ℳ\mathcal{M} on [n][n], we associate to ℳ\mathcal{M} a pseudometric δℳ\delta_{\mathcal{M}} on the network realignment graph 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} via

δℳ​(T1,T2)=∑{i,j}∈ℳ|dT1​(i,j)−dT2​(i,j)|.\delta_{\mathcal{M}}(T_{1},T_{2})=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{M}}|d_{T_{1}}(i,j)-d_{T_{2}}(i,j)|.

The matching distance of two trees is defined to be

δ⁡(T1,T2)=maxℳ​ matching on ​[n]⁡δℳ​(T1,T2).\delta(T_{1},T_{2})=\max_{\mathcal{M}\text{ matching on }[n]}\delta_{\mathcal{M}}(T_{1},T_{2}).
Lemma 3.20.

The matching distance δ\delta is a metric and

δ⁡(T1,T2)≤d𝒢n​(T1,T2).\delta(T_{1},T_{2})\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},T_{2}).

In particular, diamδ⁡(𝒢n)≤diam⁡(𝒢n)\operatorname{diam}_{\delta}(\mathcal{G}_{n})\leq\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{G}_{n}), where diamδ⁡(𝒢n)\operatorname{diam}_{\delta}(\mathcal{G}_{n}) denotes the diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} with respect to the matching distance.

Proof.

To see that δ\delta is a metric, observe that for any two distinct trees T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}, there must exist vertices i,ji,j, such that dT1​(i,j)≠dT2​(i,j)d_{T_{1}}(i,j)\neq d_{T_{2}}(i,j). Hence, if 𝒩\mathcal{N} is any matching containing the pair {i,j}\{i,j\}, then δ\delta satisfies

1≤δ𝒩​(T1,T2)≤δ⁡(T1,T2).1\leq\delta_{\mathcal{N}}(T_{1},T_{2})\leq\delta(T_{1},T_{2}).

Thus, δ⁡(T1,T2)=0\delta(T_{1},T_{2})=0 if and only if T1=T2T_{1}=T_{2}. The other axioms of a metric are obviously satisfied by δ\delta.

To see that for any two trees δ⁡(T1,T2)≤d𝒢n​(T1,T2)\delta(T_{1},T_{2})\leq d_{\mathcal{G}_{n}}(T_{1},T_{2}), it suffices to observe that δ⁡(T2,T2)=0\delta(T_{2},T_{2})=0 and that the value of δ⁡(T1,T2)\delta(T_{1},T_{2}) changes by at most one, when a leaf slide is applied to T1T_{1}. The proof of this is identical to the proof that Φc\Phi_{c} changes by at most one under a leaf slide, despite sliding the chosen vertex cc, in 3.6. ∎

Lemma 3.21.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a matching on [n][n], then for any tree T∈V⁡(𝒢n)T\in V(\mathcal{G}_{n}) we have

∑{i,j}∈ℳdT​(i,j)≤n​a−a2,\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{M}}d_{T}(i,j)\leq na-a^{2},

where a=|ℳ|a=|\mathcal{M}|.

Proof.

For an edge ee of TT, we denote by τℳ​(e)\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e) the number of pairs {i,j}\{i,j\} in ℳ\mathcal{M} for which ee lies on the unique path connecting ii and jj in TT. Then

∑{i,j}∈ℳdT​(i,j)=∑e∈E⁡(T)τℳ​(e).\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{M}}d_{T}(i,j)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e).

Further, we denote by AeA_{e} and BeB_{e} the connected components of T∖{e}T\setminus\{e\}. If ee is an edge of TT and {i,j}∈ℳ\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{M}, then ee lies on the unique path connecting ii and jj if and only if ii and jj lie in different connected components of T∖{e}T\setminus\{e\}. In particular, τℳ​(e)≤min⁡(|V⁡(Ae)|,|V⁡(Be)|)\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e)\leq\min(|V(A_{e})|,|V(B_{e})|). Additionally, it follows immediately from the definition of τℳ\tau_{\mathcal{M}} that τℳ​(e)≤a\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e)\leq a. Thus,

∑e∈E⁡(T)τℳ​(e)=∑k=1a|{e∈E⁡(T)∣τℳ​(e)≥k}|≤∑k=1a|{e∈E⁡(T)∣min⁡(|V⁡(Ae)|,|V⁡(Be)|)≥k}|.\begin{split}\sum_{e\in E(T)}\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e)&=\sum_{k=1}^{a}|\{e\in E(T)\mid\tau_{\mathcal{M}}(e)\geq k\}|\\ &\leq\sum_{k=1}^{a}|\{e\in E(T)\mid\min(|V(A_{e})|,|V(B_{e})|)\geq k\}|.\\ \end{split}

Since

∑k=1an−2​k+1=n​a−a2,\sum_{k=1}^{a}n-2k+1=na-a^{2},

all that is left to show is that for any kk there are at most n−2​k+1n-2k+1 edges ee in TT for which min⁡(|V⁡(Ae)|,|V⁡(Be)|)≥k\min(|V(A_{e})|,|V(B_{e})|)\geq k.

To see this, notice first that the set of edges satisfying this condition form a connected subgraph HkH_{k} of TT. If this subgraph is empty or consists of a single edge, then there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, HkH_{k} is a tree with at least two vertices.

Let e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} be two distinct leaf edges of HkH_{k}. Let i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Without loss of generality, we may assume that Hk∖{ei}⊆AeiH_{k}\setminus\{e_{i}\}\subseteq A_{e_{i}}. Further, since eie_{i} lies in HkH_{k}, we have |Bei|≥k|B_{e_{i}}|\geq k.

We conclude that Hk∖{e1,e2}⊆T∖(Be1∪Be2)H_{k}\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}\subseteq T\setminus(B_{e_{1}}\cup B_{e_{2}}), and thus |V⁡(Hk)|−2≤n−2​k|V(H_{k})|-2\leq n-2k, because Be1∩Be2B_{e_{1}}\cap B_{e_{2}} is empty. But this means that there are at most n−2​k+1n-2k+1 edges in HkH_{k}, which concludes the proof. ∎

Proposition 3.22.

The diameter of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} with respect to the matching distance is

diamδ⁡(𝒢n)={6​k2−2​k,n=4​k,6​k2,n=4​k+1,6​k2+4​k,n=4​k+2,6​k2+6​k+1,n=4​k+3.\operatorname{diam}_{\delta}(\mathcal{G}_{n})=\begin{cases}6k^{2}-2k,&n=4k,\\ 6k^{2},&n=4k+1,\\ 6k^{2}+4k,&n=4k+2,\\ 6k^{2}+6k+1,&n=4k+3.\end{cases}
Proof.

We give the proof in the case n=4​kn=4k, where the notation is simplest. The other congruence classes are obtained by the same argument, replacing the two blocks of kk matching pairs by blocks of sizes

p=⌊⌊n/2⌋2⌋,q=⌈⌊n/2⌋2⌉,p=\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad q=\left\lceil\frac{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{2}\right\rceil,

and, when nn is odd, leaving one vertex unmatched. This gives the formula above. Let n=4​kn=4k. We give a matching ℳ\mathcal{M}, as well as trees T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}, such that

δℳ​(T1,T2)=6​k2−2​k.\delta_{\mathcal{M}}(T_{1},T_{2})=6k^{2}-2k.

Let LL be the path tree with labels (1,…,4​k)(1,\dots,4k), and let SS be the path tree with labels

4. Automorphisms of XnX_{n}

Each permutation in the symmetric group SnS_{n} induces an automorphism of XnX_{n} by relabelling the vertices of each network realignment. In this chapter, we prove that, for n≥5n\geq 5, every automorphism of XnX_{n} arises in this way. To achieve this, we first show that XnX_{n} is fully determined by its 1-skeleton. We then identify an Aut⁡(Xn)\Aut(X_{n})-invariant subcomplex HH whose automorphism group is the symmetric group, and prove that the natural map

Aut⁡(Xn)↪Aut⁡(H)\Aut(X_{n})\hookrightarrow\Aut(H)

given by restriction is injective. The proof relies on some of the quantities introduced in Section 3.

The condition n≥5n\geq 5 is necessary. Indeed, X4=ΣK4X_{4}=\Sigma_{K_{4}}, and thus

Aut⁡(X4)=Aut⁡(ΣK4)=S26⋊S4.\Aut(X_{4})=\Aut(\Sigma_{K_{4}})=S_{2}^{6}\rtimes S_{4}.

An explanation of the second equality is given in Section 4.2. Although Aut⁡(X3)=Aut⁡(K3)=S3\Aut(X_{3})=\Aut(K_{3})=S_{3}, the argument for n≥5n\geq 5 does not apply in this case.

4.1. XnX_{n} is a Cubical Flag Complex

First, we show that XnX_{n} is determined by its 1-skeleton. Consequently, every automorphism is uniquely determined by its restriction to the 1-skeleton, implying

Aut⁡(Xn)≅Aut⁡(𝒢n).\Aut(X_{n})\cong\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n}).

Let II denote an interval and IkI^{k} a kk-cube. We write (Ik)1(I^{k})_{1} for its 1-skeleton and ∂Ik\partial I^{k} for its boundary.

A cubical complex KK is called cubical flag complex, or determined by its 1-skeleton, if any injective cellular map (Ik)1→K(I^{k})_{1}\to K admits a unique extension Ik→KI^{k}\to K, meaning that the diagram

admits a unique extension for all k≥2k\geq 2.

Note that the aforementioned property is equivalent to requiring that any injective cellular map ∂Ik→K\partial I^{k}\to K admits a unique extension Ik→KI^{k}\to K for all k≥2k\geq 2. This easily follows from an inductive argument.

Since the intersection of any two cells in a cubical complex is empty or a common face, a 2-cell is uniquely determined by any three of its vertices. This carries over to 4-cycles, as each 4-cycle is the boundary of a 2-cell. ∎

4.2. A Rigid Subcomplex

Next, we identify an Aut⁡(𝒢n)\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n})-invariant subgraph H⊆𝒢nH\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{n} whose automorphism group is the symmetric group SnS_{n}. The key idea is that any automorphism of XnX_{n} must preserve the dimension of the cubes, and thus restricts to an automorphism on Σn=ΣKn\Sigma_{n}=\Sigma_{K_{n}}, which contains exactly the (n−2)(n-2)-cubes Ci,jC_{i,j}. The only vertices of a cube Ci,jC_{i,j} that lie in another (n−2)(n-2)-cube are the star trees sis_{i} and sjs_{j}, which occur at opposite corners. The automorphisms of a Ci,jC_{i,j} fixing these two vertices form a group isomorphic to Sn−2S_{n-2}, and such automorphisms may be chosen independently for each cube Ci,jC_{i,j}. Together with the natural action of SnS_{n}, it follows that

Aut⁡(Σn)=Sn−2(n2)⋊Sn.\Aut(\Sigma_{n})=S_{n-2}^{\binom{n}{2}}\rtimes S_{n}.

Hence, to obtain a rigid subgraph HH, we must include additional cells linking distinct (n−2)(n-2)-cubes.

is well-defined.

4.3. Determining Automorphisms from Restrictions

It remains to show that the map

Aut⁡(𝒢n)→Aut⁡(H)\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n})\to\Aut(H)

given by restriction is injective. To this end, we again make use of 4-cycles. As observed earlier, every 4-cycle in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is uniquely determined by any three of its vertices. Hence, if an automorphism fixes three vertices of a 4-cycle, then it must also fix the fourth.

Lemma 4.9.

Let f:𝒢n→𝒢nf:\mathcal{G}_{n}\to\mathcal{G}_{n} be an automorphism. Let C=T1,T2,T3,T4C=T_{1},T_{2},T_{3},T_{4} be a 4-cycle in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} such that f⁡(Ti)=Tif(T_{i})=T_{i} for 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3, then f⁡(T4)=T4f(T_{4})=T_{4}.

Proof.

Any automorphism must map CC to a 4-cycle. By 4.2, the only 4-cycle that contains T1,T2,T3T_{1},T_{2},T_{3} is CC. Hence, f⁡(C)=Cf(C)=C and f⁡(T4)=T4f(T_{4})=T_{4}. ∎

More generally, automorphisms of GnG_{n} are determined by their values on any subgraph from which all remaining vertices can be recovered by repeatedly adjoining the fourth vertex of a 4-cycle whenever the other three vertices are already present. This motivates the following closure property for subgraphs.

Definition 4.10.

Let H⊆𝒢nH\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{n} be a subgraph. We say that H⊆𝒢nH\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{n} is closed under 4-cycle completion if for every 4-cycle CC in 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}

(4.1) |V⁡(C)∩V⁡(H)|≥3​ implies ​C⊆H.|V(C)\cap V(H)|\geq 3\text{ implies }C\subseteq H.

From the following proposition we can deduce that HH is such an aforementioned subgraph whose values fully determine an automorphism of GnG_{n}. This will allow us to directly determine the automorphism group Aut⁡(Gn)\Aut(G_{n}).

Proposition 4.11.

Let HH be a subgraph of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} that is closed under 4-cycle completion. If Σn⊆H\Sigma_{n}\subseteq H, then H=𝒢nH=\mathcal{G}_{n}.

We begin by introducing additional tools needed for the proof.

Let TT be a tree, and let c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} be two distinct centroids of TT. Then Fc1​(T)=Fc2​(T)F_{c_{1}}(T)=F_{c_{2}}(T).

Proof.

By 2.42, (c1,c2)∈E⁡(T)(c_{1},c_{2})\in E(T). Write T∖{(c1,c2)}=A(c1,c2)∪B(c1,c2)T\setminus\{(c_{1},c_{2})\}=A_{(c_{1},c_{2})}\cup B_{(c_{1},c_{2})} with c1∈V⁡(A(c1,c2))c_{1}\in V(A_{(c_{1},c_{2})}) and c2∈V⁡(B(c1,c2))c_{2}\in V(B_{(c_{1},c_{2})}). |V⁡(A(c1,c2))|+|V⁡(B(c1,c2))|=|V⁡(T)|=n.|V(A_{(c_{1},c_{2})})|+|V(B_{(c_{1},c_{2})})|=|V(T)|=n.

For a tree TT, define Fcent​(T)=Fc​(T)F_{\mathrm{cent}}(T)=F_{c}(T) for any centroid cc of TT. By 4.12, this is well-defined.

Now, we are ready to prove 4.11. The strategy is as follows. Theorem 4.14.

Aut⁡(Xn)≅Sn\Aut(X_{n})\cong S_{n} for n≥5n\geq 5.

Proof.

By 4.4, it is enough to show that Aut⁡(𝒢n)≅Sn\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n})\cong S_{n}. Consider the following sequence of maps:

Along the first horizontal map, an element of SnS_{n} is mapped to the induced automorphism of 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}, which relabels the vertices of each network realignment. The second and third horizontal maps are given by restriction.

By 4.8, the composition of the first two maps is an isomorphism. Injectivity of Aut⁡(𝒢n)→Aut⁡(Σn)\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n})\to\Aut(\Sigma_{n}) follows by combining 4.9 and 4.11. Therefore, the map Aut⁡(𝒢n)→Aut⁡(H)\Aut(\mathcal{G}_{n})\to\Aut(H) is bijective. By 4.8, Aut⁡(H)≅Sn\Aut(H)\cong S_{n}, and the result follows. ∎

Appendix A Equivariant Generalised Morse Theory

Now, we prove the main theorem of generalised Morse theory. The key step is to show that an interval [σ,τ][\sigma,\tau] collapses onto its complement in the cube τ\tau. By ordering the nontrivial intervals Λ\Lambda-equivariantly, we can inductively perform these collapses to obtain a Λ\Lambda-equivariant strong deformation retraction of the space onto the subcomplex formed by the critical cells.

Definition A.1.

Let τ\tau be an nn-cube, σ\sigma a proper face of τ\tau. Define

𝒲τ​(σ)=|τ|∖⋃σ≤μ≤τInt​(μ).\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma)=|\tau|\setminus\bigcup\limits_{\sigma\leq\mu\leq\tau}\textup{Int}(\mu).

Note that 𝒲τ​(σ)\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma) contains all faces of the cube τ\tau that do not contain the face σ\sigma. Hence, 𝒲τ​(σ)⊆∂τ\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma)\subseteq\partial\tau.

Proposition A.2.

Let τ\tau be an nn-cube, σ\sigma a proper kk-dimensional face of τ\tau, and let Λ\Lambda denote the subgroup of Aut⁡(τ)\Aut(\tau) that fixes σ\sigma, i.e. g​σ=σg\sigma=\sigma for g∈Λg\in\Lambda. Then, 𝒲τ​(σ)\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma) is a Λ\Lambda-equivariant strong deformation retract of the cube τ\tau.

Proof.

We identify |τ||\tau| with [−1,1]n[-1,1]^{n} such that

σ={(v1,…,vk,1,…,1)∣v1,…,vk∈[−1,1]}.\sigma=\{(v_{1},\dots,v_{k},1,\dots,1)\mid v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in[-1,1]\}.

Then, the barycenter of σ\sigma is bσ=(0,…,0⏟k−t​i​m​e​s,1,…,1)b_{\sigma}=(\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{k-times},1,\dots,1). Choose some ε>0\varepsilon>0. We define y=(1+ε)​bσy=(1+\varepsilon)b_{\sigma}. For each point x∈|τ|x\in|\tau|, we denote the line going through yy and xx by

Lx={t​x+(1−t)​y∣t∈ℝ},L_{x}=\{tx+(1-t)y\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\},

and by rxr_{x} the unique point in the intersection of LxL_{x} and 𝒲τ​(σ)\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma). Now, we can define the following homotopy

H:|τ|×[0,1]→|τ|,(x,t)↦(1−t)​x+t​rx,H\colon|\tau|\times[0,1]\rightarrow|\tau|,\quad(x,t)\mapsto(1-t)x+tr_{x},

where H⁡(x,0)=xH(x,0)=x and H⁡(x,1)=rx∈𝒲τ​(σ)H(x,1)=r_{x}\in\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma). If x∈𝒲τ​(σ)x\in\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma), then rx=xr_{x}=x, and thus H⁡(x,t)=xH(x,t)=x. This proves that 𝒲τ​(σ)\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma) is a strong deformation retract of |τ||\tau|.

It remains to show that HH is Λ\Lambda-equivariant. For g∈Λg\in\Lambda, we have g​y=ygy=y, since g​σ=σg\sigma=\sigma implies g​bσ=bσgb_{\sigma}=b_{\sigma}, and hence

(A.1) Lg​x={t​g​x+(1−t)​y∣t∈ℝ}=g​Lx.L_{gx}=\{tgx+(1-t)y\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\}=gL_{x}.

Now, gg preserves both ∂τ\partial\tau and Int(σ\sigma), and hence also 𝒲τ​(σ)\mathcal{W}_{\tau}(\sigma), which implies

Given a generalised Morse matching on a cubical Λ\Lambda-complex XX, let X/∼X/\sim denote the set of equivalence classes of ∼\sim, equipped with the relation given by the transitive closure of

[σ1,τ1]≤[σ2,τ2]ifσ1≤τ2.[\sigma_{1},\tau_{1}]\leq[\sigma_{2},\tau_{2}]\quad\text{if}\quad\sigma_{1}\leq\tau_{2}.

Since ∼\sim is acyclic, X/∼X/\sim is a poset. If ∼\sim is Λ\Lambda-equivariant, then Λ\Lambda acts naturally on X/∼X/\sim. We analyse this action in the next lemma.

Lemma A.3.

Let XX be a cubical Λ\Lambda-complex, and let ∼\sim be a generalised Morse matching that is Λ\Lambda-equivariant. Then the induced Λ\Lambda-action on X/∼X/\sim is horizontal, i.e. [σ,τ]≤g⁡[σ,τ][\sigma,\tau]\leq g[\sigma,\tau] implies [σ,τ]=g⁡[σ,τ][\sigma,\tau]=g[\sigma,\tau] for all [σ,τ][\sigma,\tau] in ∼\sim and g∈Gg\in G.

Proof.

Any order-preserving group action of a group Λ\Lambda on a finite poset PP is horizontal. Indeed, suppose there exist p∈Pp\in P and g∈Λg\in\Lambda such that p<g​pp<gp. Since the action is order-preserving, it follows inductively that

p<g​p<…<gi​p<gi+1​p<…,p<gp<\ldots<g^{i}p<g^{i+1}p<\ldots,

which contradicts that PP is finite. In particular, the induced Λ\Lambda-action on X/∼X/\sim is horizontal. ∎
